research_access_confound.what: This week's Sonnet books are systematically less researched than other tiers' — because of the desk's dispatch order, not the model.
research_access_confound.detail: The session shares one WebSearch budget of 200 calls across every manager polled. The desk dispatched by tier — Fable, then Haiku, then Opus, then Sonnet — so by the time the Sonnet managers ran, the budget was spent. Zero of the 42 Fable/Haiku/Opus books state that they did no research; at least five of the 25 Sonnet books state plainly that they decided on the packet alone, and two named the exhausted 200-call budget as the reason. Several Opus managers also hit the ceiling late and finished verification with WebFetch.
research_access_confound.why_it_matters: Research access is supposed to be identical across managers; the model tier is the experiment's independent variable. A tier-correlated difference in research capability is a confound in exactly the comparison this experiment exists to make, and it was created by the desk's own dispatch ordering. Week 12's Sonnet results should not be read as evidence about Sonnet's judgment.
research_access_confound.fix: From week 13 the dispatch order interleaves tiers instead of grouping them, so budget depletion falls evenly rather than on whoever is polled last.

decisions.reason: First reassessment in two weeks. The defensive risk-premia book is doing its job: +1.35% with a -2.39% max drawdown against a tape where 75% of S&P stocks fell in September, and no leg's thesis is invalidated by its mark. The two losing legs, GLD (-4.6%) and TLT (-4.9%, 5% weight, -8% stop), were hit by the same factor, the five-week bond rout that took the 10-year to 5.34% on 10-01 after the Fed's 09-16 hike; Friday's +29k payroll miss and 4.2% unemployment flipped CME odds to ~80% for an October hold, yields fell and the dollar dropped, which is precisely the turn both contrarian legs were sized for, so selling them now would be selling at the point of maximum pressure. EWZ (7%, +0.3%) faces Brazil's first round on Sunday 10-04, which resolves before any order I write could execute at the 10-05 close; the leg already carries the pre-election -12% stop and +10% take-profit, Brazil's fear gauge is at a record 31.8 so a lot is priced, and prediction markets (Flavio ~57%) versus polls (runoff tied) give no edge to pre-empt. UNH (-1.5%) reports 10-13 with pre-earnings caution already in the price and a 30% stop for a contrarian-value leg; BRK-B is flat with Howard Buffett now chair and Abel as CEO, business as usual; SVXY (+0.9%) is fine with VIX at 15.3 and a quiet week ahead (ISM services, FOMC minutes). No change I would make is worth more than the noise of making it, and the book keeps 46% cash at 4% to absorb the Brazil and UNH events. Zero overlap with the Round 2 momentum book is preserved.

This book was built three days ago at the 09-30 close and the week's news confirmed rather than contradicted it, so trading again would be churn I pay for twice. Leg-by-leg: (1) Managed care, my largest theme at 25% (CI 13 + CVS 12), got better not worse. CI reaffirmed 2026 adjusted EPS of at least $30.45 and a 10-14% growth target through 2030 at its Investor Day, Piper lifted its target to $370 on 10-01, BofA carries it as a top 2026 managed-care pick, and the sector bid on 10-02 as cost-trend hopes softened. At the $270.53 mark CI is 8.9x and CVS is ~10.8x the raised $7.90-8.10 guide. The 2027 setup is the thesis in one line: insurers are filing ~14% median marketplace premium increases against ~10% medical trend, which is pricing above trend and that is how MLR margin recovers. (2) Citi at $128.50 is 1.27x the $100.89 Q2 tangible book into 10-13 earnings, with consensus EPS +20.5% year over year and $30B of buyback running at roughly tangible book. That is a near catalyst I was positioned for on purpose, and selling ahead of it forfeits the reason I own it. (3) The XLP short is the leg the week strengthened most: the 10-year printed 5.34%, its highest since 2002, before easing to ~5.25%, and capital was actively leaving staples into energy and tech on 10-01. Short 21x bond proxies against a 5%+ risk-free is exactly the trade. (4) Pharma was neutral-to-positive, with a CAMZYOS pediatric label expansion and positive Phase 2 eczema data at PFE. Nothing is near a stop: the worst leg, PFE, is -2.52% against an 18% stop, and the book is only -0.20% weighted since entry, so no leg has become materially cheaper or richer than when I sized it. The one real flaw I found is worth recording rather than acting on. The energy stub (CVX 11 + XOM 8) and the XLP short are 30% of gross all leaning the same way on the Hormuz binary: a peace deal would drop oil from ~$100 and pull yields down, hurting both at once. That binary is genuinely live -- Trump said on 10-01 the war ends 'very soon, one way or the other', Qatar is mediating Iran's seven-day reopening proposal, and talks are called more serious. But I sized the damage and it is survivable, not existential: a deal costs roughly 2.6% of NAV across those legs against a 4.39% max drawdown to date, with no stop triggered, so risk management does not compel a trade. And both legs have standalone value cases independent of the macro -- XOM and CVX at 12.4-12.7x still earn at $80 Brent, and staples at 21x with no volume growth are a poor asset at any yield. Meanwhile OPEC+ is expected to hold output steady on 10-04 with ~5.7 mb/d still shut in through Q4, so the near-term supply picture supports the stub, and it is the only thing in an otherwise all-long book that pays if the war escalates into record-high index levels and a 5.3% 10-year. I would rather carry a deliberate stagflation tail hedge than strip it and be naked long defensives into an oil shock. Holding also keeps 14% cash earning 4% as dry powder for CI and BMY earnings on 10-29 and PFE on 11-03, which is when the next real information arrives. Deep value is paid for waiting through the holding period, not for re-underwriting a thesis every five sessions; the frictions and the rejection risk of rewriting a compliant eight-leg book are certain, and the expected gain from tinkering is not.

Two things changed since the 09-16 entry and they point the same way. First, the rate shock is not over: the 10-year closed 10-02 at 5.27%, the highest since 2002, the Fed hiked 25bp in September with another penciled in by year-end, and futures now price fed funds near 4.1% by January - markets are pricing tightening, not cuts. My book was built for a world where a 5% 10-year had finished repricing low-yield defensives; instead the repricing continued, and that is precisely where my losses sit (MDT -5.95%, JNJ -4.21%, SCHD -2.54%). Second, the oil thesis is intact but has moved downstream: Brent held $102.25 on 10-02 and jumped 4% on 10-01 on an extra carrier deployment, while WTI sagged to $91.11 on an emergency reserve release, opening an $11-plus spread, and US diesel cracks set an all-time record above $106/bbl. The obvious trade - pure-play refiners - is the one I am deliberately refusing: VLO is +84% YTD at $405.96 against a $348.81 consensus target and MPC +89% at $421.93 against $370.38, both trading above where analysts think they belong after six straight up weeks, and the administration is floating a diesel export ban that is the direct cause of WTI's decoupling. Buying a crowded trade above target into binary policy risk is not dividend growth. I capture the same cracks through CVX and XOM, whose downstream segments earn them at upstream-level valuations that have not run. So I fund two additions by cutting what the regime is actively taxing: MDT at 21.3x with a MiniMed spin-off losing its allure is my worst leg and has no inflation pass-through, and JNJ is a dividend king yielding under 3% against a 5.27% risk-free - the strategy of record already exited the expensive bond proxies and these are the last two. I also cut the SCHD core from 34% to 24%: not a loss of faith - at 17.9x versus the S&P's 26.4x, oversold at its $32 technical support, and the best of 14 dividend ETFs this year, it stays my largest position by nine points - but 34% in a single duration-sensitive ETF during an active rate repricing was one undiversified factor bet, and I would rather own the rate shock from both sides. Net turnover is about 24% of the book, not a replacement, so friction is roughly a dime at 2bps a side. I keep cash at 12% earning 4% because a hiking Fed at 24-year-high long yields is still compressing multiples.
decisions.strategy: Long-only dividend-growth book that keeps a reduced SCHD quality core and its Brent-linked integrated-energy and midstream tilt, and rotates the two duration-like bond proxies into dividend growers that are paid rather than punished by a 5.27% 10-year - a cheap P&C insurer reinvesting float at 24-year-high yields and a de-rated defense prime levered to the Hormuz conflict that is actually driving the inflation.

positions.thesis: Still the book's core and its cleanest expression of the mandate: the Dow Jones US Dividend 100 screen demands a decade of consecutive payments then ranks on cash-flow-to-debt, ROE, yield and five-year dividend growth, it has raised its income stream 14 straight years, and it beat all 14 competing dividend ETFs this year. At 17.87x against the S&P's 26.37x it is the cheap half of the market, and at $32.72 it sits on the $32 support with oversold RSI after a 5.7% slide from the August $35 peak. I am cutting it from 34% to 24% rather than adding, because a 5.27% 10-year with more hikes priced is a live headwind to a high-yield screen and 34% made one factor the whole book - but it remains my largest position by a wide margin and the 100-name breadth, including its own energy and financial weights, is the diversified base I rebuild around. No take-profit: this is the compounding core, not a trade.

The integrated way to own a record refining margin without paying a pure-play's post-84% price. Chevron's upstream is weighted to Brent-linked international barrels, which closed 10-02 at $102.25 and rose 4% on 10-01 on an additional carrier deployment toward Hormuz, while its downstream earns the same diesel crack above $106/bbl that has taken VLO and MPC above their analyst targets. At $206.69 it is below my 211.54 entry and has not participated in the refiner melt-up, so I am paid for the margin without the crowding or the diesel-export-ban exposure that is specifically a US-refiner risk. Nearly four decades of consecutive dividend increases funded by a commodity whose price is being set by supply disruption is exactly the hard-asset dividend growth this mandate wants. Trimmed one point only to fund sizing elsewhere. The 12% stop respects the real tail: an Iran ceasefire took oil down over 16% in a single day in April and would do it again.

The highest-conviction new idea: the rare dividend grower that the rate shock pays instead of punishing. A P&C insurer collects premiums up front and reinvests the float, so a 10-year at 5.27% - the highest since 2002 - lifts Chubb's investment income for years as the portfolio rolls, which is the precise mechanism that makes it the mirror image of the bond proxies I am cutting. It closed 10-02 at $330.89 on 11.71x earnings with net income up 21.6% and revenue up 7.7%, a Buy consensus and a $365.91 target - a double-digit grower at a single-digit-growth multiple, cheaper than MDT's 21.3x for far better momentum. Thirty-plus years of consecutive dividend increases keeps it squarely inside a dividend-growth mandate even though the 1.23% current yield is low: my mandate is growth of the payout, and a cheap, fast-compounding book value is what funds future growth. Sized at 13% as the second-largest position because the thesis is mechanical, not a forecast. Wider 13% stop because the hard-market and float story needs quarters, not days.

My only leg in the green since 09-16 (+0.42% at $164.01), and the most downstream-weighted of the integrateds - its refining and chemicals footprint is the largest among the majors, so the all-time-record diesel crack above $106/bbl lands directly in its earnings while its global upstream is priced off the $102 Brent that the Hormuz escalation keeps bid. Nudged up a point because this is the best risk-adjusted claim on the record crack available to me: unlike the pure refiners it has substantial non-US refining, which blunts the diesel-export-ban risk that is currently driving WTI's $11-plus discount, and its multiple never re-rated the way VLO's and MPC's did. Four decades of unbroken dividend increases through far worse oil tape than this. Same 12% stop as CVX for the shared ceasefire risk.

Owning the macro driver rather than only its oil-price symptom. The single fact setting my book's tape is a US-Iran conflict around the Strait of Hormuz - carriers deploying, Brent jumping 4% on 10-01 on a deployment headline - and General Dynamics' Combat Systems (ammunition and munitions) and Marine Systems (submarines and surface combatants) are the direct industrial beneficiaries of exactly that, with multi-year backlog rather than a spot price. The remarkable part is that it never rallied: at $330.09 the market cap is down 2.7% over the period while revenue rose 9.1%, net income 9.8% and EPS 10.1% to $16.40, leaving 20.1x trailing and 18.79x forward against a $420.26 Buy-consensus target implying 27% upside. A de-rating into growing earnings is the opposite of the refiners' re-rating into peak margins. Twenty-eight-plus consecutive years of dividend increases earns its place in this book, and the exposure is genuinely uncorrelated with my energy legs - a ceasefire that stops out CVX and XOM is a far smaller problem for a submarine backlog. Take-profit set at the analyst target.

Held unchanged as the book's healthcare exposure now that MDT and JNJ are gone, because it is the one of the three that is actually growing into its payout rather than acting as a bond substitute. Flat since entry at $262.82 while revenue grew 10.4% to $64.39B and net income rose 67.7%, it trades at 17.35x forward - a third of MDT's trailing multiple on vastly better growth - and the pipeline delivered in the last few weeks: FDA approval of JUVMO (tavapadon) in Parkinson's and positive Phase 3 data for etentamig in multiple myeloma, which is what pushes the immunology-successor story past the Humira erosion that created the sector overhang. The 2.63% yield is backed by growth, not duration. Only +6.1% to consensus target, so I am not adding; 8% is the right size for a leg I like but do not think is cheap. Ex-dividend 10-15 falls just after entry.

Added a point: in an energy-driven inflation shock with the Fed hiking, a midstream partnership whose pipeline tariffs escalate contractually with producer inflation is one of the few genuine real-asset income streams, and it earns on volumes rather than on the crude price - so it keeps paying if a ceasefire breaks the $102 Brent that my CVX and XOM legs depend on. That makes the 6% weight a partial hedge inside the energy sleeve, not a doubling of it. It reported record Q2 2026 EBITDA and cash flow on strong pipeline volumes, yields 6.19% at $36.18 on 12.54x earnings with a $41.48 consensus target, and has raised its distribution for more than a quarter-century. It is my second-worst leg at -5.01%, which is why I am adding modestly rather than cutting: the operating result got better while the unit price fell. Q3 earnings 10-29.

Kept at 5% as the second leg of the own-the-rate-shock-from-both-sides idea, sized small because the evidence is genuinely mixed. The case: at $57.51 it trades at 11.48x trailing and 10.50x forward with a 3.76% yield, 2025 earnings grew 21.75% on 5.01% revenue growth, and the Buy consensus target of $70.43 implies 22% upside - a large, cheap deposit franchise whose asset yields reprice upward as the Fed hikes. The caution that keeps it at 5%: JPMorgan cut its target to $65 and Truist and Evercore also trimmed ahead of the 10-15 Q3 print, and a bank at 24-year-high long yields carries securities-portfolio and deposit-cost risk alongside the margin benefit. Q3 earnings ten days after entry make this the book's clearest near-term event risk, which is exactly why it is my smallest position rather than one I either add to or abandon.

decisions.reason: Two things changed. First, my cohort read was half right and half stale. The 52-week-high and 1-month-momentum lists through 09-30 confirm the AI/software core (META +29% in September, its best month in four years; OKTA +58% 1m; CRWD +20.3% 1m at a 52wk high; AMD +33% 1m) so that half of the book stays. But the 'life-sciences TOOLS' half of my strategy of record has decayed into the laggard: TMO is at a 52wk high yet only +9.3% 1m, trades ABOVE its $619 average analyst target at a $655 mark, and sits in an end market described as budget-constrained through all of 2026; MTD is not on any new-high list at all. The actual acceleration in that complex is in genomics/therapeutics - TXG +50.7% 1m, TWST +46.3% 1m, GRAL +75.6% 1m, alongside MRNA +47.4% and NTRA +27.1% which I already own. So I cut MTD outright, cut TMO to a 4% residual, and redeploy into the part of the cohort that is actually trending. I also cut ABBV (defensive pharma, on no momentum list) and AAPL (cleared its prior high by 0.29%, the weakest mega-cap trend I own) - 17 points of non-momentum ballast in a momentum book. Second, and this is the part that stopped me from doing the obvious thing: the loudest momentum signal on the tape is a trap at the margin. The SOX has run 18 straight up days for +44%, the longest streak in its 32-year history, and sits more than 50% above its 200-day moving average - a reading not seen since 2000 - on an 85 RSI, with the move explicitly attributed to call-buying and gamma squeezes in AMD and MU. A naive re-rank would have me max out semis on the day after NVDA's first record since May. I will not. I keep semi exposure and add NVDA at only 10% (it has the cleanest trend plus a real $150B buyback bid under it) while TRIMMING AMD from 13 to 10 because it is the named squeeze vehicle, and I skip FORM (+56%) and VICR (+64%) entirely despite their being the top of my own screen - those are the froth most likely to round-trip violently. The redeployment goes mostly to genomics instead, which is early in a base breakout rather than 50% above its 200dma. Cash to 12% from 10% because FOMC minutes land Wednesday 10-07 with hike risk genuinely live (ISM manufacturing prices-paid printed 77.9 vs 72.3 expected) and high-multiple momentum is what gets hit if those minutes read hawkish. Net: I am staying with the trend, paying for one real re-rank, and refusing to chase the single most extended cohort in 26 years.
decisions.strategy: Concentrated long-only US price momentum that keeps its AI-levered tech core but deliberately refuses to add into the historically extended semiconductor blow-off, and rotates the life-sciences sleeve out of the budget-constrained tools names into the genomics/therapeutics names that are the ones actually printing accelerating 1-month returns.

positions.thesis: Top weight and earned it: +29% in September, the strongest month in about four years, on the Meta Muse AI-agent launch that flipped the narrative from bearish to bullish. It gave back ~4.8% into month-end after a 37% run, which is consolidation inside an intact trend, not a break - and re-rating from 18x to 23x forward earnings is a re-rating the market granted, not a stretch. Size held at 15 rather than raised because the easy multiple expansion is now behind it.

The cleanest large-cap trend in the market: first record high since May, nearing $6T, +14% since 09-14 on AI demand and a $150B buyback authorization - the largest single increase in corporate history, which is a standing mechanical bid no screen captures. Deliberately only 10% and not larger: it is leading a cohort trading >50% above its 200dma, so this is trend participation, not a bet on the blow-off continuing. 15% stop is tight relative to the cohort's realized vol precisely because I want to be taken out early if the streak breaks.

TRIMMED from 13 to 10, which is the single most considered decision in this book. AMD is +33% over the month, cleared its prior 52-week peak by 8.6%, and is already +3.6% for me since the 09-30 fill - pure momentum says add. I am cutting instead because AMD is named specifically as a vehicle of the aggressive call-buying and gamma squeeze driving the SOX to a 26-year extreme. Gamma-driven moves unwind far faster than they build. I keep a real position because the trend is real; I shrink it because the marginal buyer is an options desk, not a fundamental one.

Raised from 9 to 10. Up 58.2% over the last month and the largest name on the mid-cap new-high list at ~$36.4B, which is the exact signature my mandate screens for - fresh 52-week high with accelerating 1-month return - and it sits in identity/security rather than semis, so it carries none of the SOX extension risk. 20% stop reflects genuinely higher realized vol than the mega-caps after a move that size.

Raised from 8 to 9. One of only six large caps at a 52-week high on 09-30 and +20.3% over the month - a steadier slope than the parabolic names, which is what I want more of, not less, with the chip complex this stretched. Cybersecurity spend is the least discretionary line in an enterprise software budget, so the trend has a fundamental floor under it that MTD and ABBV do not.

Held at 7. The strongest one-month run on the large-cap new-high list at +47.4%, and I am explicit that this is a price-momentum holding and nothing else: revenue declined 27.7% over the trailing twelve months. That divergence is exactly why the weight stays small and the stop stays wide at 25% - wide enough not to be shaken out by the volatility a move like this generates, small enough that being wrong about a fundamentally deteriorating business costs me under 2% of the book.

Raised from 6 to 7. At a 52-week high with +27.1% over the month at ~$59B, and unlike MRNA the momentum is attached to a growing diagnostics franchise rather than a shrinking revenue line. It is the highest-quality trend in the genomics cohort I am rotating toward, so it gets the larger of the two 7% slots.

New. 10x Genomics, +50.7% over the month and the strongest one-month run on the mid-cap new-high list, at ~$11.6B. This is the leg that most directly replaces MTD: same life-sciences end market, opposite momentum. Where the tools names are rangebound against a budget-constrained customer, single-cell and spatial genomics is where that constrained budget is actually being spent. Small size and a wide 25% stop because it is a post-de-rating name whose daily range is large.

New. Twist Bioscience, +46.3% over the month at ~$12.5B, a second independent confirmation that the genomics breakout is a cohort move and not one stock's news. I am sizing TXG and TWST equally at 6 rather than concentrating in one, because when I am buying a group rotation I want the group, not a single-name bet inside it - synthetic DNA and single-cell tools can diverge sharply on company-specific execution.

New, and the smallest leg at 4% on purpose. GRAIL is +75.6% over the month at ~$5.9B - the most violent trend I am willing to own, in multi-cancer early detection where the move is binary on screening-test adoption and reimbursement. Momentum this steep in a pre-profitability diagnostics name is the definition of a position that should be small with a wide 28% stop: enough room that normal noise does not close it, small enough that a full stop-out costs ~1.1% of the book.

CUT from 8 to a 4% residual rather than closed. The bull case is intact enough to keep a toe in - it is at a 52-week high, it raised 2026 guidance on better customer activity and operating leverage, and it is weathering the biopharma spending pullback better than its peers. But +9.3% over the month is the weakest momentum of anything I am keeping, a $655 mark sits above the $619 average of 23 analyst targets, and the end market stays suppressed through 2026. In a book whose mandate is to own accelerating trends, that earns a residual, not a core weight. The 12% stop stays tight because this is the leg I am least willing to defend.

decisions.reason: Researched with WebSearch (budget was still live, so this is real research, not a packet-only call) and every leg came back confirmed rather than contradicted. The leg is three sessions old (filled 09-30) and no company-specific news has arrived for any of the five names since that fill. V: core payment volumes at records and stablecoin settlement up 15x year-over-year, with the 09-30 Open Standard/OUSD consortium putting Visa on the issuing side of the disintermediation it is supposed to fear; the DOJ antitrust and swipe-fee overhang is real but unchanged and already priced into a 22% weight. NVDA: new all-time high, ~$5.7T cap, Morgan Stanley reinstated it as top semi pick; the circular-deal/OpenAI-financing critique is the live bear case and is exactly why it is 20% and not 30%, with a -20% stop. TSM: AI demand described as exceptionally strong, FY26 capex raised to $60-64B, Q3 prints 10-15 with a quiet period opening 10-05 - I am not resizing into a blackout. CME: record September AND record Q3 average daily volume across rates, equities, energy, ags, FX, metals and crypto, earnings 10-21; the thesis that CME earns more from the rate volatility that threatens the rest of the book is the one leg this week's macro actively validated. GOOGL at 14% is the one name that fails my own stated screen - 2026 capex guided to $195-205B, Q2 free cash flow of -$5.9B, zero buyback, $49.6B of stock/convertible preferred and $20.3B of notes issued - but that is precisely why I already halved it on 09-30 and it is not new information. Finishing that exit now would mean I misjudged three days ago, not that anything changed; the honest trigger is Q3 in late October showing a second negative-FCF quarter, and until then the -18% stop enforces the discipline for me. The only genuinely new information this week is macro: cooler-than-expected PCE on 10-01 and a 29K September payroll print on 10-02 collapsed October Fed HIKE odds from ~70% to ~17%, while a December hike stays priced. That setup is mildly good for this book as constructed - lower yields support the long-duration franchises, the live December debate keeps CME's volume engine running - and the stalling labour market is the one argument for trimming V, which I am noting rather than acting on at a 22% weight with records in the underlying business. 17% cash at 4% is the right dry powder into a TSM print on 10-15 and a contested December FOMC. Decisive mechanical reason not to churn: this schema only permits HOLD or a full replacement book, so moving a single stop would re-register all five legs at the 10-05 close, discarding a favourable basis (NVDA +2.44%, TSM +3.64%, V +0.37%, CME +0.44%) and re-anchoring every stop and take-profit to a higher fill. A quality-compounder mandate on leg 9 of its history does not need a tenth leg to re-price its own stops upward for no new reason.

I came in expecting to redeploy cash and the research argued the other way, so I am standing still. The book is three sessions old (entered 09-30) at 70% gross / 30% cash, NAV +5.48% vs SPY +3.80%, and every leg is doing what I bought it for: CRDO +12.2% (Q2 revenue $479M, +114.7% YoY, EPS $1.20 vs $1.17), ALAB -1.6% but with revenue +104% YoY and Scorpio-X in volume production ahead of schedule, HOOD flat with BTIG/KBW flagging better-than-expected Q3 metrics, September crypto volume the highest since February, event contracts +17% MoM, the Treasury trustee mandate for Trump Accounts, and sell-side targets clustered at $134-150 against a $112 mark. Nothing in the three theses broke, so there is nothing to replace. The temptation was the 10-02 payrolls miss, which cut October hike odds to near zero and would normally weaken the hiking-cycle rationale behind my 30% cash. But the tape says the opposite: the 10-year closed at 5.27% on 10-02, the highest since 2002, and it rose THROUGH the soft print. That is a fiscal and term-premium selloff, not a growth-expectations one, and it is the single worst configuration for long-duration small/mid-cap growth multiples: discount rates climbing for reasons monetary easing will not fix, while the labor data that would normally rescue earnings is itself softening. Rate risk did not leave the book, it changed hands. So the de-risk I did last week is more justified today than it was when I did it, and 30% cash at 4% is a position I am actively choosing, not neglect. Against that, replacing has a specific cost beyond the 2bps: re-entry resets my fills and the stop cushions underneath them. CRDO's stop sits at ~146 off a 194.79 fill; re-entering near 219 drags it to ~165 on a name whose 52-week range is 86-309, converting a survivable drawdown into a stop-out. I will not pay that to buy a stock I already own 12% higher than I bought it. Adding a fourth AI-infrastructure leg is also the wrong diversification: CRDO and ALAB are already 48% of the book on one factor (hyperscaler connectivity capex, with CRDO's top three customers at ~88% of revenue), and cash is currently the only thing in here that is not that trade. I also note ALAB now carries two-sided sell-side flow (Northland cut to Market Perform on valuation, Barclays on UALink share) but its driver is shipped revenue, and the Nov 10 print, not an analyst note, settles it. Catalysts are all ahead of me and none need a new position: ALAB Nov 10, CRDO Dec 2, HOOD's Q3 print, plus live S&P 500 inclusion optionality in ALAB. Holding is the active call this week.

The book (VZ, MO, C, BTI, PFE, 32% cash) was rebuilt on 2026-09-08 and sits at +0.66% NAV. No leg is near its stop (VZ is worst at -8.9% against an 18% stop) and none is near take-profit. Deep-value dividend theses play out over quarters, not weeks. A replacement would cost 2-12bps per side and force realized losses on VZ and C with no new catalyst. I did not run new web research this week, so there is no fresh evidence that a thesis broke. The 32% cash already earns 4% APY as ballast. Holding beats churning.

Checked the packet marks plus web research on the macro backdrop and on MO. Q4 commentary (geopolitical conflict, high oil, elevated bond yields) favours defensive staples/healthcare dividend payers and an energy hedge, which is exactly the book's tilt; CVX (+11%) is the hedge working. The laggards are MO (-7.8%, about 8% under its fill versus a 20% stop; weak trend on falling cigarette volumes and dividend-durability worries, but earnings are not until 2026-10-29 and the yield and valuation of roughly 14x P/E give some cushion) and NOBL (-4.1%, far from its 15% stop). No stop is near, no leg is closed, and I found no new thesis-breaking news on JNJ, KO, PG or ABBV. Lagging SPY (+3.8%) is a style effect of the defensive mandate, not a signal to abandon it. Any replacement trade would cost 2bps per side plus spread and would mostly swap one dividend payer for another, so holding beats churning.

The mandate's core premise was confirmed by the tape this cycle rather than broken, so there is nothing to fix. The September 2026 FOMC raised the target range 25bp to 3.75-4.00% -- the first hike since 2023 -- and the median dot carries one more 25bp hike into year-end (4.1%), flat through 2027, with no cuts until 2028. That is precisely the configuration this book was built for: JAAA and ICLO are top-of-capital-structure AAA CLO floaters whose coupons reset upward off SOFR with each hike, while the engine's cash rate is pinned at a fixed 4%. AAA CLO spreads sit around 127bp, so the floater sleeve is earning roughly 5.2-5.3% and ratcheting higher in December, against 4% for idle cash -- about 125bp of pickup that widens, not narrows, from here. Trading out of 66% in floaters into anything else right now would be selling the one asset whose contract terms improve on the next Fed move.

No leg is impaired. The book filled three sessions ago on 2026-09-30 and every position is flat-to-positive: JAAA +0.02%, ICLO +0.04%, AMLP +1.48%, SPYI +0.81%. Not one stop is remotely threatened -- the -8% stops on the CLO legs are many multiples of what AAA paper moves in a quarter, which is a feature of the sizing, not a reason to re-cut it. AMLP is up about 20.7% total return year to date on a ~7.7% yield with fee-based pipeline cash flows and LNG/data-center gas demand behind it, so the energy-inflation hedge is doing its job; its +25% take-profit is still far above the 51.87 fill. SPYI marks near 53.60 against a 53.28 print on 10-01, so the packet's marks are credible, and the early-October pickup in index volatility raises the premium that 8% variance-selling sleeve collects.

I did consider two live refinements and rejected both on arithmetic. First, pushing the 10% cash buffer into JAAA to harvest the 125bp spread: that is +12.5bp annualized on the whole book, roughly a quarter of a basis point per week, against 2bp of commission charged today -- an eight-week payback to surrender my only dry powder, with the book re-polled weekly anyway. Second, upsizing floaters by trimming SPYI on the hiking path: same shape, certain immediate cost against a few tens of basis points of annualized carry. A carry book's edge is measured in basis points per week, which makes churn the fastest way to destroy it; a full replacement of this $1,000 book burns something like half a week of coupon to end up holding substantially what I already hold.

The real temptation this week is the scoreboard, not the portfolio: NAV is -2.43% against SPY +3.80% and BTC +32.23%. But that gap was created by earlier legs in this book's nine-leg history, including a standing-order BTC fill, and it is sunk. Reaching for beta or crypto to close it would convert a floating-rate carry mandate into something I was not hired to run, at the exact moment the carry trade's macro backdrop turned favorable. I also note that a book rejected on a technicality leaves the previous book standing regardless -- so an optional, marginal trade carries real rejection risk for no expected gain, while holding four verified, currently-listed tickers carries none.

On credit risk, which is the one thing that could genuinely hurt a 66% CLO position: the stress showing up in late-2025 and 2026 is concentrated in private credit, subprime auto and PIK-toggle direct lending -- Tricolor and First Brands are the names -- with roughly 40% of private credit borrowers at negative free cash flow. That stress sits well below me in the structure. No AAA CLO tranche has ever defaulted across nearly 7,000 tranches issued since 1993, and US CLO collateral defaults are projected to fall toward 3.0% from 5.3% a year earlier. A credit wobble widens AAA spreads a few basis points and dents price by fractions of a percent while raising my forward coupon; it does not threaten principal at the top of the stack. I am comfortable carrying this book into the 2026-10-05 close unchanged.

Three things changed in the 48 hours since this leg filled, and each hits a named premise of the book of record. (1) The regime label is stale. My strategy of record was built for a 'Fed-hiking' regime; the 10-02 payrolls print (29k jobs, unemployment up to 4.2%) cut October hike odds from 64% to 16% and the policy path is now genuinely two-sided -- weak labor against 3.7% headline PCE, with the Fed itself not forecasting 2% until 2029. That is stagflation, not tightening, and it re-ranks my legs rather than invalidating the structure. (2) Two legs are fundamentally impaired, both on the low-income consumer, which the weak jobs print makes worse rather than better. LVS is printing fresh 52-week lows on Macau hold and VIP softness with a Hold consensus -- I am cutting it to zero rather than holding a long whose residual is moving against me for fundamental reasons. DG's trade-down thesis is broken by DG's own management, which flagged 'spending exhaustion' and rural customers limiting trips on elevated fuel; the stock is -22.6% over three months and its next print is not until December, so it carries impairment with no catalyst inside my window. Trimmed 5.0 to 3.0 rather than zero because it is already heavily de-rated at ~16x. (3) TRV carries a dated adverse catalyst I did not own when I sized it. A late-September Northeast nor'easter hit Travelers harder than any other listed P&C carrier given its mid-Atlantic and Northeast commercial and personal lines concentration, and Q3 lands 10-16 -- inside this holding period. The stock is up since my fill, so it is not priced. Cutting 6.0 to 2.5 and tightening the stop to 12%. Against those cuts I am concentrating into the two residuals that hard data confirms rather than reaching for new names: CME 7 to 9 on record September ADV of 31.8m contracts (+22% y/y), record Q3 ADV, rate ADV +22% and Treasury futures +42% -- the one thing the jobs shock unambiguously raised is policy volatility, and CME monetizes it with the quarter's volumes already banked ahead of its ~10-21 print and the 10-27/28 FOMC; and NEM 4.5 to 8 on gold above $4,500, record quarterly FCF, and dovish repricing into 3.7% inflation pushing real rates down, which is the cleanest macro-confirmed residual I own. These two are low-beta and uncorrelated with each other (exchange volumes vs bullion), so the concentration does not cost me dispersion breadth. I examined CF Industries as an orthogonal inflation-levered add and rejected it: +55% YTD with neutral analysts and a specific late-2026 China urea-flood risk fails my own screen. I kept SPY as the hedge instrument rather than switching to equal-weight RSP, which I considered seriously: with top-10 concentration at a 50-year extreme and the Cboe implied-correlation index resuming its decline, shorting the cap-weighted index against a non-mega-cap basket is an intended part of this book's edge, not an accidental factor bet. I am staying fully inside the dispersion mandate and not drifting directional -- net index beta is ~-0.2% of NAV. Structurally this is a deliberately good moment to be long single-stock dispersion against short index: constituent implied vol has compressed since late July while implied correlation falls into the October earnings cycle (Q3 season opens 10-08, banks 10-13/14, consensus +29% EPS growth), the seasonal window when the constituent-minus-index vol spread widens. Total turnover is ~20% of NAV, which at 2bps equity frictions costs a few cents -- this is a surgical repositioning, not the full churn the book of record would have cost. Eleven weeks at +0.63% with roughly zero beta-adjusted alpha is the honest reason I am not simply holding: the structure is right, the leg-level composition was not.

positions.thesis: The book's anchor because it is the one leg where I think the distribution is genuinely mispriced. BHF closed 10-02 at 50.02 against Aquarian Capital's signed $70 all-cash merger; stockholders have approved and every condition except Delaware, New York and Massachusetts insurance approval is satisfied or waived. The spread is 40% because Delaware's regulator questioned founder Rudy Sahay behind closed doors about where Aquarian's capital comes from and how it would manage the balance sheet, and the Sept 6 outside date auto-extended to Dec 6. The reason to be long is what that price implies: BHF was about $45 pre-deal in Nov 2025 and equity markets are materially higher since, which lifts its variable-annuity book, so standalone worth is now plausibly around here. At 50 I am paying roughly standalone value and getting the $70 nearly free, plus a second call option - Talcott Financial, backed by Sixth Street, sent the board a private letter reaffirming it wants the company if Aquarian falls through, after a reported $55 approach. Outcomes cluster at $70 on a close, mid-50s on a Talcott takeout, mid-40s only if both fail. Sized at 34% because the downside is largely already in the price, not because the upside is large. The 36% take-profit sits just under $70 so a close is banked at the print rather than left to a delisting; the 22% stop is deliberately wide, at roughly $39, so a forced-unwind gap on a break does not sell me the bottom while a funded rival is waiting.

Trimmed from 17% but kept as the only live non-deal catalyst and the book's sole inflation hedge. Brent settled near 99.68 and WTI near 91.24 on 10-02, Hormuz traffic remains far below pre-war levels, and the US is weighing a second carrier into the region, so the supply-disruption premium is intact and unresolved rather than spent. Expressing it through XLE keeps the money in producers - XOM, CVX and COP are about 48% of the fund - instead of refiners whose cracks compress when crude spikes. It also hedges the right risk: with headline CPI at 3.4% and the Fed hiking, energy is what works if inflation stays sticky, which is the scenario that hurts everything else I own. Trimmed because the leg has already been paid - XLE is up 44.6% over twelve months and sits within 5% of its 52-week high of 66.17 - so a credible ceasefire headline is a fast drawdown. Hence the stop tightened to 10% from 12%.

Kept as uncorrelated carry, cut to the size the spread actually justifies. Arcosa stockholders approved CRH's $150 all-cash acquisition on Sept 4; only regulatory clearance remains and the close is guided to Q1 2027. At 146.50 that is a 2.39% gross spread over roughly four months, about 7% annualized against 4% on cash, so the real excess is under a point - which is exactly why this is 11% and no longer the book's largest position. What it still earns is independence: a shareholder-approved cash deal does not care what the Fed does on Oct 28, and that is worth holding beside a 34% position whose own risk is also regulatory, because the two regulators are unrelated. The live risk is US aggregates overlap drawing a DOJ second request now that the Division has revived targeted second requests. No take-profit, since the most this can pay is par; the 8% stop is set to trigger only on an actual break rather than on spread noise.

decisions.reason: Two things changed and both argue for resizing rather than holding. First, SNPS is no longer a mean-reversion position. The 30 Sep Investor Day (FY27 revenue ~$11.15B, ~15% growth, ~44% non-GAAP operating margin, ~$1B buyback) plus the OpenAI GPT-Synopsys partnership and a >$1B Amazon IP pact drove a 12.8% single-day gain on 1 Oct and a +16% eight-day streak, with HSBC upgrading to Buy and lifting its target from $490 to $700. My thesis - an EDA leader that raised guidance into its own selloff - is not just priced, it is fully reversed, and the stock is now the most extended name I own. Holding it at a 16% top weight is momentum, which is someone else's mandate; symmetrically, an eight-day +16% run is exactly the kind of stretch my book is supposed to sell into. I harvest half to 8% and keep the rest as paid-for optionality on the structural re-rate. Second, and the reason this is a trade rather than a hold: my stop geometry had gone stale. Stops are evaluated against entry fill, so after three sessions SNPS's -16% stop sat near 365 against a 489.90 mark - 25% below the market, meaning no protection at all - and CSCO's and XYL's stops were similarly slack. Re-entering the whole book at the 5 Oct close resets every stop tight around current prices, which is worth the roughly 4bps of round-trip friction on a $1,000 book. On the names I keep, the news is better than when I entered, not worse. The 3-session flatness in LMT and GD is noise, not disconfirmation: the House passed a continuing resolution 370-48 funding defense at FY26 levels through 11 Dec, removing shutdown risk; the White House has summoned the primes over depleted Patriot and Tomahawk stockpiles; LMT lifted its 2026 forecasts into Pentagon restocking with a ~$230B backlog and UBS at $674; GD carries a $136.5B backlog, a 1.5-to-1 aerospace book-to-bill and a Jefferies upgrade on the submarine boom. XYL is the purest setup I have left - it printed a new 52-week low at 100.17 after I bought it, but the overhang is now definitively resolved rather than merely priced, because the $1.5B of senior notes was launched and priced on 15 Sep across 2029/2032/2037 maturities on top of a committed $1.5B bridge, fully funding the $1.46B Cornell/Roper purchase that closes in Q4. I add to both. What I deliberately did NOT do is reach for the fresh crop of oversold large caps, and that is the main research output of the week. New 52-week lows beat new highs for ten straight sessions and only 25% of the S&P sits above its 50-day, the lowest since April, so the screen is full - but every candidate fails my one distinguishing test. HD and LOW are housing names whose cause, a 5.25% 10-year, is live and worsening. TMUS is at a two-year low with JPMorgan and Scotiabank still cutting targets ahead of an unreported Q3, and its churn problem is self-inflicted and ongoing; the $18.2B buyback and Deutsche Telekom merger report that would be the reversal catalyst are from April and stale. PEP hit a 52-week low on an Evercore downgrade with earnings on 8 Oct, three days after my entry - a binary I have no edge in. UNH's DOJ criminal and civil probes are open-ended with no resolution timeline. Oversold for a reason that is still running is not my trade, so the capital those names would have taken stays in cash at 4% instead, and gross comes down from 75% to 73%.

positions.thesis: The cleanest version of my mandate: a de-rating caused by a headline, running directly against fundamentals that are accelerating. LMT sits roughly 25% below its March 2026 peak near $693 because the US-Iran interim peace agreement compressed the geopolitical risk premium across the complex, not because demand fell. The opposite happened - the war depleted Patriot interceptor and Tomahawk stockpiles faster than planned, LMT has lifted its 2026 forecasts into Pentagon restocking, PAC-3 bookings have been running at multi-billion quarterly rates, and the backlog is at a record ~$230B. At roughly 17x NTM earnings it is the cheapest large-cap defense name on both earnings and EV/EBITDA, and UBS carries $674 against a 505.41 mark on ~9% revenue growth through 2028 from missiles, munitions, F-35 sustainment, CH-53K and Trident. The remaining overhang - framework production agreements that cannot be fully funded without full-year appropriations - now has both a floor and a date: the continuing resolution funds weapons programs at FY26 levels and Congress has until 11 Dec. I hold this at top weight because the de-rate is sentiment and the restock is contractual. The honest bear case is the Q1 swing to negative free cash flow against $6.5-6.8B full-year guidance, plus fixed-price contract risk, which is why the stop is 12% rather than wider.

Added from 11% because it offers the same peace-premium de-rate as LMT with better backlog visibility and less fixed-price exposure. GD fell about 3.5% in the sector-wide peace-deal unwind - selling that was explicitly sector rotation rather than company news - and has not recovered, sitting at 330.09 against a $423 average analyst target, about 28% higher. Behind that sits a $136.5B backlog concentrated in Marine Systems, where US Navy submarine demand is structurally strong and the unit is beating internal expectations, prompting a Jefferies upgrade on the submarine boom. Aerospace is running a 1.5-to-1 book-to-bill with margin expansion and improving Gulfstream G700 deliveries, so the cycle is being confirmed by orders, not forecasts. Submarine and Gulfstream revenue is also among the least rate-sensitive cash flow in large-cap industrials, which matters more than usual with the 10-year at 5.25%. I size it just under LMT because the de-rate is shallower, so the snapback is smaller, but the earnings path is better underwritten.

Added from 11% because this is the one leg where the drawdown cause has moved from priced to actually resolved. XYL printed a fresh 52-week low at 100.17 on balance-sheet fear after it lined up funding for the $1.46B cash purchase of the Cornell Pump and Roper Pump businesses from Indicor. That fear is now answered by completed transactions rather than promises: a committed $1.5B 364-day senior unsecured bridge facility from a bank syndicate, and $1.5B of senior notes launched and priced on 15 Sep across 2029, 2032 and 2037 maturities, which terms out the bridge and fully funds the deal and related costs ahead of a Q4 2026 close. The financing risk the market sold is the financing that has already been raised at a known cost. What is left is a water-infrastructure compounder with a utility-capex demand base, bought at the exact bottom of its 52-week range, where the marginal seller was a credit worry that no longer has anything to worry about. Held at 11% because the thesis is resolving exactly as written and is not yet finished. I bought a network incumbent marked down by price-target cuts while its revenue accelerated; the acceleration has since been confirmed, with fiscal Q4 2026 product orders up 35% year over year and AI infrastructure orders driving a 3.56% gain on 2 Oct, and the leg is +4.65% from a 107.21 fill. I do not add, for two reasons: the stock is up about 46% in 2026, so the oversold condition that made it a mean-reversion candidate is largely gone, and one-year implied volatility at 36.7% is high for a name whose remaining upside is target catch-up. Cut from 16% to 8% - a deliberate harvest, not a loss of conviction. The mean-reversion trade worked completely in three sessions, +12.64% from a 434.94 fill to 489.90, and the cause I bought has fully reversed: the 30 Sep Investor Day guided FY27 to ~$11.15B revenue on ~15% growth with ~44% non-GAAP operating margin and ~$1B of near-term buybacks, paired with a >$1B multi-year Amazon IP and tools pact and an OpenAI partnership to build GPT-Synopsys into the EDA and agentic platforms, and HSBC upgraded to Buy with its target going from $490 to $700 on earnings growth accelerating toward 28% annually through 2028. That is a structural re-rate, and it is precisely why the position has to shrink: an eight-day +16% run makes SNPS the most extended name I own, and a book whose edge is buying stretched-to-the-downside quality has no business carrying a stretched-to-the-upside momentum leader at top weight. I keep a half position because the fundamental news is real and the partnerships are multi-year, so there is a genuine path toward the HSBC case, but I am now risking a banked gain rather than a discount. The 12% stop against a fresh 5 Oct fill is the specific fix for the problem that forced this trade: on the old basis the stop sat near 365, a full 25% below the market, which protected nothing.

Held at 10% as the book's smallest and most idiosyncratic leg, with its thesis corrected. HON is no longer the aerospace-and-automation conglomerate I first underwrote: the Aerospace spin-off completed on 29 Jun 2026, with holders receiving one share of Honeywell Aerospace (HONA, Nasdaq) for every two HON shares, leaving HON as Honeywell Technologies across three automation-focused segments. What I own is therefore a post-spin automation compounder still trading with the de-rating and index-driven selling that follows a large separation, where the holders who wanted the aerospace asset have sold and the automation story has not yet been re-underwritten on its own numbers - a classic structural, non-fundamental seller, which is the kind of drawdown cause my mandate wants. The leg is +1.45% from a 210.94 fill, so the re-rating has barely begun. I keep it small rather than add: post-spin price discovery is genuinely noisy, the remaining company has less of the munitions-restocking exposure that made the original story attractive, and automation capex is more rate-sensitive than defense backlog with the 10-year at 5.25%. The 16% take-profit is the tightest in the book because the upside here is re-rating to fair value, not a deep discount closing.

decisions.reason: Two changes, one conviction and one correction. CORRECTION: I am retiring the M/KSS department-store pair because its premise did not survive re-reading the filings. I built it on a guidance divergence, but both names RAISED full-year guidance - Macy's lifted sales, comps, EBITDA and EPS guidance on 2026-09-10, and Kohl's also raised its FY outlook on 2026-08-26 to $1.80-2.40 EPS with gross margin up 305bps, a restarted buyback of up to $100M and a maintained dividend. The real gap was only comp quality (M +2.7% vs KSS -0.9%, where the KSS beat leaned on roughly $150M of one-time tariff refunds), a far thinner edge than I had sized it for. Worse, the short leg is the most crowded short in consumer discretionary: KSS short interest was 29.4% of shares outstanding and about 41% of float as of 2026-10-01, rising off a ~24% trough in late September after the stock nearly tripled from its April lows, and it has a Reddit-driven squeeze in its history. Paying 3% borrow to stand in front of 41%-of-float short interest, in a company that is raising guidance and expanding gross margin, to harvest a 3.6pp comp difference is the wrong side of a convexity trade - a squeeze costs multiples of the fundamental edge and would blow through an 18% stop in a single session. That pair was also the losing half of the book, roughly -0.31% net across its two legs since the 09-30 fill. CONVICTION: I am sizing the steel pair up from 15/15 to 20/20 because it has an unusual property going into earnings season - BOTH legs have already pre-released quarterly guidance (STLD on 09-17, NUE for its quarter ended 10-03), so the 10-19 and late-October prints are largely de-risked and what is left to trade is the forward divergence rather than a surprise. REPLACEMENT: the airline pair restores a genuine directional divergence - raised versus cut - with a short leg that is liquid and not crowded. Net effect: gross 60% to 70%, cash 40% to 30%, the book stays close to market-neutral, and total friction for the switch is well under $1 on a $1,009 book, so churn is not the binding consideration - idea quality is. I omit take-profits deliberately: stops and TPs are evaluated per leg against my entry fill, so a TP firing on one leg would orphan the other and convert a hedged pair into a naked directional bet. Stops are wide and symmetric within each pair for the same reason.
decisions.strategy: Two equal-weighted, same-industry relative-value pairs built on dated company-specific guidance divergences - long STLD / short NUE in steel and long UAL / short AAL in airlines - run at 70% gross with 30% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: Long leg of the steel pair, upsized from 15% on a forward catalyst NUE does not have. STLD's 09-17 guidance of $5.34-5.38 read as a headline miss against roughly $5.60 consensus and the stock sold off, which is where my 09-30 fill at 221.61 came from; the contents were better than the headline - record shipments, metal-margin expansion across the platform, and higher realized selling values against lower scrap costs. Two company-specific drivers run past this quarter: a steel-fabrication backlog nearly 50% above prior-year Q3 that extends through Q1 2027, and the Columbus, Mississippi aluminum flat-rolled mill, where all three cold mills are operational and the first CASH line ships commercial material in Q4 2026 - a new earnings stream starting now. Because STLD pre-guides, the 10-19 print should land near a number already public, so I am paid for the forward divergence rather than exposed to a surprise.

Short leg of the steel pair, matched at 20% so the trade expresses company-specific divergence rather than a view on hot-rolled coil. NUE guided its quarter to $5.55-5.65, but the composition is weaker than STLD's: steel mills and steel products improve on higher realized pricing while Raw Materials deteriorates on both lower pricing and lower shipments, and NUE has no ramping new-capacity earnings stream comparable to STLD's aluminum mill - its incremental dollar comes from price, a shared industry input I am hedging out, not an idiosyncratic one. Holding it short also caps the pair's exposure to a steel-price reversal, which is the main way the long leg could be wrong for reasons that have nothing to do with STLD.

Long leg of the new airline pair and the cleaner half of a raised-versus-cut divergence. United raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $9-11 even while absorbing nearly $6 billion of additional 2026 fuel expense - the strongest form of my strategy's signal, a company guiding up into a cost shock, which argues the margin gain is structural (international network, premium cabin, loyalty) rather than cyclical. At $112.51 on the 10-02 close that is roughly 11-12x the guided range, and UAL was nearly flat in September (+0.3%) while Delta ran +4.5%, so unlike DAL this leg has not already paid out its divergence; I chose UAL over DAL for that reason even though Delta's Trainer refinery is the better fuel hedge. Earnings are 10-20, after next week's poll, so I am not entering blind into a print. Sized at 15% rather than 20% because this pair carries oil-price basis risk the steel pair does not.

Short leg of the airline pair, and the specific name that guided DOWN in the same cost shock UAL guided up into: American cut full-year adjusted EPS to a range spanning a loss, -$0.65 to +$0.65 from -$0.40 to +$1.10, and guided its September quarter to an adjusted LOSS of $0.10-0.70 despite forecasting 16-19% revenue growth. That gap between record revenue and zero earnings is the thesis - AAL assumed about $3.75/gallon fuel versus United's $3.69 and Delta's $3.15, the thinnest cushion in the group, and with an $8.57B equity cap sitting on a far larger debt stack its equity is a thin sliver that absorbs margin pressure disproportionately. September confirmed the direction: AAL -2.4% to $13.32 while UAL was flat and the JETS sector ETF fell 3.3%. Critically, unlike the KSS short I am retiring, AAL is a large-float, cheaply-borrowed, lightly-crowded short rather than a 41%-of-float squeeze candidate. At $12.94 it sits under $15 so I pay the 12bp commission tier, about $0.18 on a $150 leg, which does not change the case. Earnings 10-22. The stop is wide at 20% to match the long leg and avoid orphaning the pair on a sector-wide fuel-relief rally, which is the main risk here: if crude collapses, AAL is the highest-beta beneficiary in the group.

decisions.reason: Two things changed between the 09-30 fill and the 10-02 close, and they point in opposite directions on the two halves of this book. First, the seasonal window I pre-committed to is now genuinely open and I am under-exposed to it: October is the best month of the year in midterm years (avg ~3.0% on the S&P, higher gains frequency than any other month), Q4 of midterm years has averaged ~5.6% since 1930 versus ~2.9% for Q4 generally, the record $1.3T buyback authorization window reopens from Oct 15, and CTA equity positioning has already been cut hard, which is the setup that turns a seasonal drift into a squeeze. Sitting at 70% gross with 30% cash through the single best statistic in my mandate is why this book is -0.41% while SPY is +3.80%; that is a process error, not bad luck, so I am deploying the dry powder into the statistic rather than holding it for a cheaper entry that the calendar says is unlikely to come. Second, the rate-shock half of the book lost its catalyst. The September payroll printed +29k against +84k expected with unemployment up to 4.2%, October hike odds collapsed, and the 2-year fell 6bp; the Fed-path short (IEF, the belly) is now fighting the data instead of riding it, so it goes. XLU goes too, for a different reason: short utilities is no longer a fresh idea but a crowded one after ~30% underperformance versus the S&P, with put/call flow flipping to calls and strategists openly calling it for a bounce - that is a short I want to be out of before the mean reversion, not during it. What I keep on the rates side is only the long end, and only small: if the Fed pauses into still-elevated inflation the curve bear-steepens, which hurts the 30-year specifically, so TLT short survives at a reduced 10% as the book's rate expression and its hedge against the equity beta I just added. I am adding IWM because small caps give the cleanest exposure to this exact statistic (midterm-year Octobers average +3.5%, higher in 83% of instances since 2002) and they come in beaten up, -7.2% on the quarter and ~9% off the August high, so the seasonal tailwind meets a washed-out tape rather than a stretched one. Refiners stay and get slightly larger because that leg is working for the reason I wrote down: Goldman now models US refiner diesel margins near $50/bbl in Q4 on products export losses of ~4mb/d, consensus 2026 Brent has been marked up to ~$89 from ~$85, and distillate seasonality is independently positive from October into January, so the seasonal and the catalyst agree. Net effect: gross 70% to 86%, rate-short gross 28% to 10%, and the book's risk moved from a rate-shock bet into the calendar bet my mandate is actually about. I am keeping 14% cash at 4% so that October - the most volatile month of the second half - can be bought into rather than only endured.
decisions.strategy: Lean into the midterm-year October/Q4 statistic now that the calendar window is actually open: raise index and small-cap beta, keep the distillate-seasonality refiner legs where the Hormuz catalyst is landing, cut the Fed-path rate shorts the weak September payroll broke, and keep one small long-end steepener plus a modest Uptober crypto leg.

positions.thesis: The core expression of the mandate's single strongest statistic, upsized from 12% because the window is now open rather than approaching. October is the best month of the midterm year (~3.0% average) and Q4 of midterm years averages ~5.6% since 1930, roughly double the all-years Q4. Three live mechanics support the statistic this cycle rather than just the average: the $1.3T record buyback authorization re-opens its execution window from Oct 15, CTA/systematic equity exposure has already been cut so the marginal flow is a buyer, and the 10-02 payroll miss takes the October hike off the table, which removes the specific shock that was capping multiples. 22% is the largest single leg but it is index beta, not idiosyncratic risk, and the 7% stop is tight enough that a genuine seasonal failure - the midterm-October pattern breaking - takes me out for under 1.6% of the book.

The highest-quality version of the same seasonal bet, and new to this book. Midterm-year Octobers have averaged +3.5% on small caps with gains in 83% of instances since 2002, and November is nearly as strong (+3.1%, positive in all six instances), so the pattern is both larger and more reliable down-cap than in the S&P. Crucially the entry is not stretched: the Russell 2000 fell 7.2% in Q3 and sits ~9% below its August high after rising yields punished floating-rate small-cap balance sheets, so I get the seasonal tailwind on a washed-out tape instead of on a momentum extension. The 10-02 payroll miss cuts both ways here - it is the leg most exposed if weak labour becomes an actual earnings problem rather than just a Fed-path story - so I size it at 12%, half the SPY leg, and set the stop wider at 9% to respect small-cap volatility without letting the position become the book's dominant risk.

The best seasonal-AND-catalyst leg in the book and already +4.8% from the 09-30 fill, so I am adding to a winner where the reason is intact rather than taking the profit. Distillate cracks are seasonally strong from October into January as heating demand builds and autumn maintenance pulls supply, and this year that calendar sits on top of a genuine supply shock: global refined product exports are running ~4mb/d below pre-war levels with the Hormuz disruption dragging on, and Goldman now models US refiner diesel margins near $50/bbl for Q4 against $37 in Europe. Valero is the most distillate- and export-levered of the large US refiners, so it is the cleanest way to own that specific margin. I keep the wide 14% stop because refining equities are high-beta to crack prints and a tight stop would be noise-stopped out of a thesis measured in months, and the 30% take-profit reflects that a Hormuz normalisation headline is the one event that ends this trade abruptly.

Same distillate-seasonality-plus-Hormuz thesis as VLO, held as a pair so the book owns the Q4 US refining margin rather than one company's operational luck - a single unplanned turnaround at one refiner should not decide whether the leg works. Marathon adds the largest US refining footprint by capacity and a midstream earnings stream that cushions the downside if cracks mean-revert faster than the seasonal suggests. It is the book's best performer at +6.8% in two sessions, which is informative rather than a reason to trim: the margin data is being revised up, not down, and consensus 2026 Brent has been marked to ~$89 from ~$85 over the past month. Sized at 10%, marginally under VLO because it is the less distillate-levered of the two, with the same 14% stop and 30% target so the pair is managed as one risk.

Held unchanged at 6% as the upstream complement to the refiner pair, and deliberately not upsized. The crude leg of the Hormuz story is working - consensus 2026 Brent marked up to ~$89 from ~$85, WTI to ~$83.90, and the leg is +2.2% - but refiners, not producers, are where the actual catalyst is landing, because the shock is in products supply rather than in crude availability. XLE earns its place by being the leg that pays if the conflict escalates to crude supply itself, which is precisely the scenario in which the equity beta I just added would be falling; it is partly a hedge on the SPY and IWM legs. A 10% stop is tighter than the refiners' because XLE is more directly a price-of-oil position and a de-escalation headline hits it first and hardest.

Kept and modestly upsized from 7% as the sector expression of the midterm-Q4 statistic, where financials are historically among the stronger Q4 performers and where a dated catalyst arrives inside the holding window: big-bank earnings open reporting season in mid-October, the same week the buyback execution window reopens, and banks are the largest single source of those repurchases. The rate backdrop also now helps rather than hurts this leg in the configuration I expect - a Fed on hold with a long end anchored near 5.3% is a steeper curve and a better net interest margin than the flattening the September hike produced, which is the same bear-steepener view the TLT short expresses, so the two legs are coherent. The leg is flat (+0.2%) since the fill, so I am adding at essentially my own cost rather than chasing. 9% stop sits just outside normal sector noise.

The only rates leg I keep, cut from a 28% three-leg rate-shock complex to a single 10% long-end short, because the half of the thesis that survived the payroll print is the term-premium half, not the Fed-path half. A Fed that pauses with inflation still elevated is the textbook bear-steepener: the 2-year rallies on the pause while the 30-year - already at 5.57% and carrying the fiscal supply burden - does not follow, which is exactly where a short expresses itself. I hold this at reduced size and not larger because the counter-evidence is real and recent: TLT rebounded on 10-02 and the signals that a bond selloff is ending are being flagged, so this is a position I want sized to survive being early rather than to be the book's main bet. It also earns its keep as the hedge against the 55% long equity beta I just added, since the scenario that breaks SPY and IWM into year-end is a renewed yield spike. 3% borrow cost is cheap for that insurance; the 8% stop caps the cost of being wrong at under 1% of NAV.

A second, genuinely independent calendar statistic for a seasonality book, which is the whole point of holding it alongside the equity legs. October is bitcoin's strongest month on record - higher in 10 of the last 13 years with an average near 18-20% - and that is a larger and better-documented seasonal edge than anything in the equity calendar. The entry is also not extended: BTC closed September near $83.5k and trades in the mid-$80ks, having gone sideways rather than parabolic into the window, and market-implied odds of a $100k October have collapsed from 85% to 13%, so the seasonal is being priced out just as it opens. I size it at only 6% for two reasons: 35bps per side makes crypto spot the most expensive thing in this book to own, and October 2025 is the live precedent for how a single macro shock cancels Uptober, with $19bn of leveraged liquidations in one session. 6% spot with a 14% stop means the tail scenario costs under 1% of the book, while a median Uptober pays multiples of that.

decisions.reason: All seven time-series signals, re-checked through the 2026-10-02 close, are still on the same side they were when this leg filled on 09-30. My system has nothing to act on, and because the only amendment format available is a full replacement, the cheapest correct action is none: paying churn across the whole book to re-establish the same positions is a real cost with no signal behind it. The week's one real event was Friday's 29k payroll miss with unemployment at 4.2%, which collapsed October hike odds from 70% to 14% and, on the narrative, breaks the 'hiking Fed' half of my macro thesis. The tape says otherwise, and the tape is what I trade: on the most dovish catalyst of the quarter TLT still closed DOWN 0.30% at 77.48 and ITB still closed DOWN 0.84% at 86.64. Both of my shorts went my way on the single worst possible day for them, which is the cleanest out-of-sample test of this book I am going to get. The curve bull-steepened (2y -10bp, 30y only -4bp), which is exactly what the 20+ year sector does when soft growth lands on top of ~$100 Brent: term premium and inflation expectations dominate the long end, so stagflation is not a long-bond bid. TLT sits 5.4% below its 50dma (81.90) and 9.4% below its 200dma (85.52); RSI 27 is a real bounce risk, and I accept it inside a -10% stop on a 26% weight, which caps the leg at 2.6% of book. ITB at 86.64 is a shade above a 52-week low of 84.81 and down 18.8% over a year, with affordability still the binding constraint at a 6.65% mortgage and builders buying rates down to 4.99% to move product -- order books defended with margin, which is how a downtrend in builder earnings persists even as rates ease. XLE at 62.70 is at 52-week highs against a 50dma of 57.51 and a 200dma of 53.90, the cleanest trend in the book and already +2.15%; the dovish repricing is a tailwind to it, to USO and to BTC, not a threat. BTC near 84.4k holds above all four key moving averages with an 11.7% cushion over the 74.3k 200d EMA. So the only legs the Fed repricing genuinely argues against are the 16% ITB short and the 6% UUP long, and against those stand 42% in XLE, USO, BTC and SPY that it helps: the net regime shift across the book is close to a wash, and nowhere near enough to override price. I re-ran the leg I cut last week as a discipline check and it confirms the cut rather than reversing it -- gold at 4,218 is still below both its 50dma (4,373) and its 200dma (4,636) with the August rally having failed at 4,720 and lower highs since, so there is no long re-entry. It now screens as a marginal short, but a stagflationary supply-shock tape with official-sector bid underneath is the wrong place to be short a real asset, and I will not replace a whole book to bolt on my weakest-conviction signal. UUP is the leg I am watching hardest: DXY at 102.02 is still +3.15% on the month and +4.40% on the year, so the trend holds, but a Fed priced out of hiking is dollar-negative and the -6% stop is deliberately the tightest in the book and will do its job without my help. One scheduled event argues specifically against trading into Monday: OPEC+ meets 10-04, the day before my fill, with a rollover of October targets the base case. That is 29% of my book in XLE and USO pricing a two-sided headline I cannot handicap better than the market can, and the right response to an event I have no edge on is to carry the exposure I already own rather than re-size into it at a fresh cost basis. The book is -2.37% against SPY +3.80%, which is the expected shape of short-duration, short-housing positioning in a melt-up tape rather than evidence of broken signals -- max drawdown is only -3.87% and six of seven legs are green on this leg. Overriding an intact system three trading days into a fresh fill because of one payroll print is the canonical way trend books die. Holding.

I was wrong about the shape of my book, not the theme. The packet reads as seven diversified positions; it was one position. All four refiners, the product tankers, the JETS short and the XRT short were the same trade - long a wide refined-product crack - because the two shorts were not hedges: cheaper jet fuel lifts airlines and cheaper diesel lifts retail, so 77% of gross was aligned one way on a single spread. That spread is now the explicit target of coordinated state action. On 10-02 the G7 agreed to release 100mb of oil and diesel over four months with the diesel release EXPEDITED into the first 20 days, Europe agreed to a French proposal for 50mb of diesel plus 50mb of IEA crude, and margins had already fallen 7% on 10-01 on the talk alone. The tell that changed my mind is that margins fell even as Chinese refiners suspended all October product exports - a genuinely bullish shock that the market sold. That is a market that has stopped paying up for tightness. Meanwhile Iran has tabled a seven-day Hormuz reopening plan with a US response pending, and my old book had no leg that survived a deal. Two things argue against abandoning refining outright and are why I keep 35%: the export ban that Bloomberg estimated would strand 29% of US diesel output was formally ruled out on 10-02, removing the real tail risk, and 7-8 mb/d of refining capacity is still offline, which a product reserve release does not repair - the 2022 analogue is that a 180mb SPR release did not stop margins staying historically wide. So this is a deliberate tilt, not a reversal: I cut gross from 86% to 62%, cut refining from 69% to 35% keeping only the names with non-refining earnings, and buy the normalization with airlines where estimates and capacity have already been cut and Q3 prints land inside the holding window. Banking PBF at +11.45% and the JETS short at +3.00%, and cutting STNG because it was flat at +0.02% for two weeks while its own driver set records - a position that will not move when its thesis is working has no claim on capital, and it is the most Hormuz-sensitive leg I own.
decisions.strategy: Halve the one-factor refining-crack bet into the G7's coordinated diesel release: keep 35% in only the lowest-crack-beta refiners, take the other side of the same spread with 27% long airlines whose fuel relief is quantified by management, drop the tanker and both crack-aligned shorts, and hold 38% cash as the only asset that wins if the whole fuel-crisis premium deflates on a Hormuz deal.

positions.thesis: Trimmed from 20% to 15% but kept as the largest refining leg. MPC is the lowest-risk way to stay long the physical margin: MPLX midstream distributions and the sector's largest buyback mean a meaningful share of cash flow is not a function of the 3-2-1, so its crack beta is below the pure refiners. It is also the most direct beneficiary of the 10-02 removal of the diesel export ban, which would have forced US refiners to cut crude runs by nearly 2 mb/d. Entering after whatever Monday reprices, with a 12% stop and a 25% take-profit that reflects a crack already at a record ~$69 rather than one with room to double.

The only leg I am increasing on the refining side, from 10% to 12%, precisely because it is the least pure refiner of the four. Midstream, chemicals and marketing carry a large share of PSX earnings, so if the expedited G7 diesel release compresses distillate margins over the next 20 days PSX gives up the least of the group, while it still participates if the offline capacity keeps margins elevated into 2027 as the EIA's timeline for Middle East supply implies. This is the defensive core of the refining allocation.

Cut hard from 18% to 8%. VLO is the best operator in US refining and I want residual exposure in case 417 kb/d of released diesel proves trivial against a 28 mb/d market with 7-8 mb/d of capacity down. But it is also the purest large-cap expression of the crack staying 3-5x normal after the group more than doubled in 2026, which is exactly the exposure I am shrinking. Deliberately a tail-position size: enough to participate if I am early, too small to define the book.

Flipped from 8% short to 17% long - the core of the reassessment and now my largest single leg. Airlines are the cleanest beneficiary of the spread the G7 is attacking: the USGC jet crack hit a monthly record $72.51 in August against a normal near $15, and jet fuel averaged $3.72/gal, 84% above a year earlier. Carriers have already cut capacity and sell-side estimates have already come down, so the bar is low into mid-October Q3 prints that land inside this holding window. Using the ETF rather than single names so that a fuel-relief rally is not derailed by one over-levered low-cost carrier's balance sheet. A 16% stop is wide on purpose - this is a thesis leg and I do not want to be shaken out of it by one headline on the Hormuz talks going the wrong way.

The quantified version of the JETS trade and the only new name in the book. United has publicly stated it would finish above the HIGH END of its adjusted EPS guidance for both Q3 and the full year if fuel prices merely return to early-July levels, after absorbing a $6bn increase in its fuel bill - management handing me the operating leverage to the exact move the G7 release is engineering, with a dated catalyst in the October print. I prefer UAL to Delta here specifically because Delta owns the Trainer refinery and is partly self-hedged, so it captures less of the fuel decline, whereas UAL is unhedged into it. Sized at 10% rather than larger because that same unhedged leverage cuts both ways if the release fizzles and distillate re-tightens; an 18% stop respects the beta.

decisions.reason: The regime call in the book of record was right and the instruments were wrong. I said the real volatility in this regime is rates, and the tape confirmed it hard: MOVE 108 after a ~30% one-week jump, the 10y at 5.24% (a 19-year high), while VIX closed 15.31 and the S&P closed at a record 7,666. But I expressed that view with a 76%-gross, six-position book that earned nothing (-0.99% vs SPY +3.80%) and with two legs that were filler rather than regime expressions. Three things changed my thinking this week. (1) The 10-02 payroll print - 29k against an 84k forecast, 60k of downward revisions, unemployment 4.2% - converts this from an inflation regime into a stagflation regime, with core PCE still 3.4% and a Warsh Fed that hiked to 3.75-4% and guides to one more. That makes the duration short two-sided at a 19-year yield high, so I cut TLT from 18% to 12% rather than pressing it. (2) I checked the VIX curve before upsizing convexity and it killed my own plan: 116 consecutive days of contango with VIX3M at 17.6 against spot ~14-15, and the extreme-complacency signal historically resolving in 3-9 months, not in my holding period.
