I had drafted VIXY at 14%; paying that roll bleed for a catalyst outside my window is how this book lost money being clever, so VIXY stays an 8% defined-cost option, not a core holding. (3) The better way to be short complacency has no carry cost: the Russell 2000 has 32% of its debt at floating rates against 6% for the S&P 500, is already down over 6% this quarter, and is the first casualty of a 5.24% long end plus a 29k labor market. So I drop XLV and VLUE - a defensive healthcare sleeve and a generic value factor are not volatility-regime expressions and XLV was my only loser - and concentrate into energy long versus small-cap and duration short. Net exposure is only about +18% but internal dispersion is high, which is the correct shape for a vol book when the macro is stagflating and equity implied vol refuses to price it.
decisions.strategy: Stagflationary vol-dispersion book: long the supply-shock inflation that is physically happening (energy equities, broad commodities), short the two most rate-and-labor-sensitive assets (small caps, long duration), with a small defined-cost VIX tail and 22% cash at 4% - low net exposure, high internal dispersion.

positions.thesis: The one inflation trade with a physical cause rather than an expectation: Strait of Hormuz disruption to over 20% of seaborne oil, Brent near 97 and up roughly 19% on the month, S&P energy earnings forecast +57% for 2026, XLE +28% YTD and +9% over 30 days against a roughly flat SPY. Sized up from 17% to the book's conviction leg because this is realized supply-shock inflation and it is the engine behind the 3.7% headline the Fed is hiking into. Held at 28 rather than higher out of respect for the named gap risk - a durable Hormuz ceasefire would compress the geopolitical premium fast - which the 13% stop bounds to under 4% of book.

New leg and now the primary way this book is short equity complacency, chosen over more VIX exposure specifically because a short has no roll decay against 116 days of contango - I pay 3% borrow instead of several percent a month in carry. The mechanism is concrete: 32% of Russell 2000 debt is floating-rate versus 6% for the S&P 500, so a 5.24% long end compounds directly into small-cap interest expense, and a labor market adding 29k jobs with 60k of revisions removes the growth offset that let small caps shrug off rising yields earlier in 2026. Already down over 6% this quarter and underperforming by the widest margin since 2020, so the trend is confirmed rather than anticipated. It also pays in the hard-landing tail where VIXY pays and the TLT short loses, which is what makes this book something other than a one-way inflation bet.

Held unchanged at 12%. Broad commodity roll exposure diversifies XLE's equity beta inside the same inflation thesis: if a ceasefire headline compresses the risk premium in oil equities, it should hit energy share prices faster and harder than the broad commodity complex, and COMT carries no single-sector earnings or buyback sensitivity. This is the inflation-linked real-asset sleeve doing its job, and at +0.43% it has no thesis damage to answer for.

Cut from 18% rather than held or pressed, which is the single biggest change in risk here. Short duration still belongs: the Fed hiked to 3.75-4%, 16 of 18 participants expect another this year, swaps imply about 70% odds for October, and core PCE at 3.4% with oil near 97 keeps feeding the long end. But I am now short a bond at 5.24%, the highest 10y since 2002, reached after a 30% one-week MOVE spike and already retreating from the high - most of the hawkishness is in the price, and the 29k payroll print makes a flight-to-quality rally a live tail rather than a theoretical one. Halving it keeps the carry and the regime exposure while cutting what is now a crowded, two-sided position at an extreme.

Kept small and deliberately not upsized. The mispricing is real - VIX 15.31 and falling with the S&P at a record, a 19-year high in long yields, core PCE 3.4%, a shooting war on a fifth of seaborne oil and payrolls at 29k - but the instrument bleeds: 116 straight days of contango with VIX3M at 17.6 over a ~14-15 spot means persistent negative roll, and the complacency signal historically resolves over 3-9 months rather than inside a weekly book. So this is sized as the premium on a defined-cost option that pays multiples in a genuine spike, with the 80% take-profit set to monetize a move toward VIX 30, not as a position expected to carry the book. The wide 25% stop is intentional - a tight stop on a decaying hedge just guarantees paying the premium and losing the optionality.

decisions.reason: Three of last week's stated reasons were falsified by the tape, so I am trading the reasons, not the P&L. (1) I had HALVED the gold complex because it was 'losing to a hiking Fed.' On 10-02 September payrolls came in at +29k with unemployment up to 4.2%, October hike odds collapsed to ~17% on FedWatch, yields fell and gold rose. The specific condition I halved gold for has been removed, and gold is -7.45% on the month to ~$4,140 inside a +65% year with sell-side targets at $4,400-5,723. That is a correction in an intact bull market, not a broken trend, so precious metals go from 14% to 30% with the operating leverage in GDX/SIL rather than all in bullion. (2) I doubled energy to 28% behind a 're-escalating' Hormuz shock. It is de-escalating operationally even without a deal: Brent fell from ~$108 on 09-28 to $99.68 on 10-02, Gulf exports have rebounded to ~21.8mb/d via alternate routes, and there have been no coalition strikes for 26 operational periods and no Iranian attacks on host states for 24-28 days. The payoff is now badly asymmetric against me, because the June 14 deal headline knocked Brent down 4.7% in a single session. I cut the sleeve to 14%, keeping only XLE for HSBC's 'structurally impaired' flows and the post-midterm escalation optionality, and drop XOP entirely as the highest-beta claim on spot crude. (3) My own strategy called the QQQ short 'anti-concentration against a 1999-style narrow tape' - which is a position that bleeds precisely when it is right. The tape was right and I was short it: Nasdaq closed at a record 27,190 on 10-02 on a record in Nvidia and a semis revival after Micron. I will not pay to fight the strongest trend in the market, so the short is gone. The honest problem for a book called Broadening is that US equal-weight breadth is deteriorating - RSP is on track for a SEVENTH straight weekly decline and the top 10 are near 40% of the index - so I trim RSP and COWZ rather than add to a losing trend, and redeploy into the places where non-mega-cap leadership is actually being confirmed: hard assets, and the industrial/electrical build-out that AI capex is funding.
decisions.strategy: Broadening expressed where broadening is actually happening: precious-metals miners re-expanded now that the Fed has stopped hiking, an industrial/power sleeve riding AI capex as it spills out of mega-cap tech, a trimmed equal-weight and free-cash-flow value core, energy cut back as the Hormuz war premium decays, a small curve-steepener in regional banks, and the losing anti-concentration QQQ short removed.

positions.thesis: Largest leg and the core of the reassessment. I cut gold last week explicitly because a hiking Fed was beating it; the 10-02 payroll miss (+29k, u-rate 4.2%) cut October hike odds to ~17% and removed that exact headwind. Miners give operating leverage to a $4,140 gold price that has already taken a 7.45% monthly correction, so I am buying the dip in the one trade that has structurally beaten my book all year rather than the top. Wide 20% stop because miners are high-beta to bullion and I want to survive noise, not get tapped out of the thesis.

The mandate leg, deliberately trimmed from 18% rather than abandoned or added to. Equal-weight is working off a seventh consecutive weekly decline against the cap-weighted index, so averaging down into it would be fighting a confirmed 7-week trend. But concentration at ~40% in the top 10 is a genuine late-1990s analogue and mean reversion pays this leg violently when it comes, so I keep a real position and let the trend, not my conviction, size it. Tighter 10% stop than my other longs because this is the leg whose premise the tape is currently contradicting.

Free-cash-flow yield is the most defensible version of the broadening trade with the 30-year at 5.59%: when capital genuinely costs 5.6%, companies that already generate cash do not have to come to the market for it, while long-duration promises get repriced. Trimmed from 16% in sympathy with the same weak-breadth evidence that trimmed RSP, but held at size because this is a valuation leg, not a momentum leg.

Energy survives as a 14% core, down from a 28% sleeve, and XOP is cut entirely. Reason to keep some: no ceasefire exists, Hormuz flows are still structurally impaired below the pre-war 19-20mb/d, a third carrier group arrives late October, and Trump has signalled renewed action could resume after the 11-03 midterms. Reason not to keep 28%: Brent has already given back $108 to $99.68 while exports recovered to ~21.8mb/d, so I am being paid less and less to hold the escalation lottery ticket, and integrateds carry reserves and downstream rather than pure spot beta.

Doubled from 6% and now my cleanest expression of broadening that the tape is actually confirming. Micron's blowout and the semis revival say the AI capex cycle is real and accelerating, and the spend leaks out of the Magnificent Seven into the power generation, grid and electrical-equipment names XLI owns - the second derivative of concentration is broad industrial demand. European rearmament at $639bn of 2026 NATO-Europe spending and Germany's 25% budget increase adds a second, independent order book. Deliberately chosen over utilities, which I would otherwise want for the same power theme but which a 19-year-high long end punishes as bond proxies.

Bullion as the lower-volatility half of a re-expanded precious-metals position, sized so the sleeve is not purely equity-beta via miners. A paused Fed, a falling dollar on 10-02 and a +29k payroll print with unemployment rising to 4.2% is the textbook configuration for gold, and this leg keeps the exposure if mining equities trade with the stock market instead of with metal.

Small, high-conviction curve-steepener. The single most reliable consequence of what happened on 10-02 is a steeper curve: the front end repriced dovishly to a ~17% October hike while the 30-year sits at 5.59%, a 19-year high driven by term premium and deficit supply rather than policy. Regional banks earn that spread directly through net interest margin. Held to only 6% because the same soft labour market that steepens the curve is also a credit risk for exactly these lenders, so the position is sized for the macro to be right and the credit to be wrong.

Small convex tail on the precious-metals thesis. Silver miners carry both monetary demand and genuine industrial demand from grid and solar build-out, which ties this leg to the same electrification theme as XLI, and they historically out-run gold miners late in a metals upcycle. Sized at 4% with a wide 22% stop precisely because the volatility is the point: I want the right tail without letting it drive the book.

decisions.reason: This book's two biggest ideas both needed work this week, in opposite directions. The Japan leg is an outright error I am correcting: last week I switched EWJ from currency-hedged to UNHEDGED specifically so 'the BoJ tightening cycle pays us in yen.' The BoJ then hiked 25bp to 1.25% in September, the highest policy rate since 1995 and the shortest interval between hikes since 1990 - and the yen WEAKENED past 157 to the dollar while JGB yields slipped and the Nikkei rose 1.5%. That is the precise opposite of the mechanism I bought, and it is not a one-day fluke but the established pattern of this cycle: Japanese equities rally on normalisation while the currency keeps sliding. Unhedged exposure donates that equity gain back through the yen, so I switch to DXJ and take the Japanese equity upside with the currency hedged out, which also tilts me toward the exporters and financials that BoJ normalisation actually helps. The TLT short is the opposite case - right leg, wrong stated reason. I justified it as shorting duration 'into a Fed that is hiking again,' and on 10-02 the Fed stopped: a +29k payroll print and a soft inflation report took October hike odds to ~17%, yields fell and the dollar dropped. But that repriced the FRONT end, and TLT is 20+ year paper. The 30-year closed at 5.59% on 10-02, a 19-year high, up 34bp in a month, and it is being driven by term premium, deficit supply and AI capex competing for capital - none of which the Fed pausing fixes, and a Fed that pauses with inflation still a risk steepens the curve, which is short-TLT-positive. So I keep the leg and raise it to 18%, on the correct thesis this time. Elsewhere I reverse one trim: I had cut emerging markets 'against a firming dollar,' and the dollar is now falling on a paused Fed, so VWO goes back up. KIE's thesis was that insurance is geared to a 5.5% long end; the long end printed 5.59%, so that leg is simply confirmed and stays. I am staying out of Brazil: its general election first round is 10-04, one day before my entry fills, and re-entering a binary the day after it resolves but before I can see the result is a coin flip, not a view.
decisions.strategy: Broadening owned outside the US index-structure trade: short the long end for term premium and deficit supply rather than for Fed policy, Japan switched back to currency-hedged because the BoJ's hikes are weakening the yen rather than strengthening it, European rearmament and international developed value as the equity core, insurance collecting a confirmed 5.6% long end, and emerging markets restored against a dollar that is now falling on a paused Fed.

positions.thesis: Raised from 16% on a rewritten thesis. The short is not a bet on the policy rate - the Fed just paused, with October hike odds down to ~17% - it is a bet on the long end, where the 30-year closed at 5.59% on 10-02, a 19-year high and 34bp higher in a month. That move is term premium, Treasury supply against persistent deficits, and AI capex bidding for the same capital, and a central bank that stops hiking while inflation risk lingers steepens the curve rather than rescuing 20+ year duration. Note also that the cost of carry runs my way: a short pays 3% borrow while idle cash earns 4%. Stop at 10% because a genuine growth scare is the one thing that would bid long bonds hard, and the 4.2% unemployment print says that risk is live.

Direct correction of last week's mistake, replacing unhedged EWJ. The BoJ hiked to 1.25% in September, its highest since 1995, and the yen still weakened past 157 while the Nikkei gained 1.5% - so Japanese equity strength and yen weakness are arriving together, and unhedged exposure hands the equity gain back in the currency. DXJ hedges the yen out and is tilted to dividend-paying exporters and financials, both of which are the actual beneficiaries of normalisation: exporters earn more in yen terms as it slides, banks earn more as domestic rates finally rise off zero. The 10-29/30 BoJ meeting with an Outlook Report is the next catalyst, and on this cycle's evidence a hawkish surprise there helps this leg and would have hurt the one I am replacing.

Raised from 12% because this is the leg whose fundamentals got better while its price did not - it is my only losing position whose order book is independently confirmed. NATO Europe is set to spend ~$639bn in 2026 with well over a third on procurement and R&D, Germany's 2026 budget earmarks ~EUR108bn for defence, a 25% year-on-year increase, and it is targeting 3.5% of GDP by 2029, six years early. NATO's own Secretary-General has warned manufacturers cannot keep pace with demand, which is the definition of pricing power for Airbus, Rolls-Royce, Safran, MTU and Rheinmetall. Multi-year legislated budgets are about the least Fed-sensitive revenue stream available to me, which is exactly what I want alongside a duration short.

International developed value is the ex-US core of the broadening mandate and gets a direct tailwind from 10-02: the dollar fell as hike odds faded, and unhedged ex-US value translates a weaker dollar straight into returns. Value also carries far less of the index-concentration risk that makes me uncomfortable owning the US tape here - this is the portion of the world's equity market that never participated in the 40%-top-ten problem. Held flat at 12% rather than raised because the same soft-growth data that weakens the dollar is not good for cyclical value earnings.

Thesis confirmed rather than revised, so the position stands. I bought this geared to a 5.5% long end; the 30-year printed 5.59% on 10-02 at a 19-year high. Insurers reinvest float into that curve, so every month the long end stays here mechanically raises forward investment income on a book they have already written, and a 2026 of elevated catastrophe and war-risk loss activity supports the pricing cycle on the underwriting side. This is also the natural long partner to the TLT short: both legs profit from a long end that stays high, so they express one macro view through two different balance sheets.

Restored from 10% because the reason I trimmed it has reversed. I cut emerging markets against 'a firming dollar'; on 10-02 the dollar fell outright as October hike odds collapsed to ~17%, and a Fed that has stopped hiking is the single most important variable for EM, which borrows and prices in dollars. EM is also the largest pool of equity in the world trading at a discount with no exposure to US index concentration, which is the mandate in its purest form. Keeps me diversified away from the developed-market rate trade that dominates the rest of this book.

Small broad developed ex-US position held as the neutral ballast of the book. It is deliberately the only leg here with no sharp thesis: EFV expresses the value factor, DXJ the hedged Japan call and EUAD a single sector, and if my factor and currency judgements are wrong but ex-US equity still beats a concentrated US index, this leg collects that. Kept at 6% so it dilutes rather than drives.

decisions.reason: Low-turnover reweight, not a rebuild: every leg of the 2026-09-30 book was confirmed by this week's tape, so I kept all six symbols and changed sizes, which costs a fraction of a full replacement. What changed is three things. (1) A leadership complex I did not own got confirmed: the AI trade is visibly rotating from compute scarcity to electricity scarcity, and GE Vernova is the measured price leader of it (+51.7% YTD, 116 GW gas backlog, heavy-duty turbine slots sold out to 2031, 2026 guidance raised to $44.5-45.5bn). A cross-sectional momentum book that owns the chips but none of the power that runs them is only half-expressing the regime, so GEV enters at 7%. (2) The duration short is now a crowded short rather than a fresh signal. The 10y printed 5.33% and the 30y 5.67%, both 24-year highs, then yields RETREATED on 10-02 as cooler PCE cut October hike odds from ~51% to ~39%. I stay short TLT because the hiking regime is intact, but I cut it 15% to 10%: the easy part of that move is behind me and the squeeze risk from a 24-year extreme is asymmetric against me. (3) I funded the additions by spending cash, not by selling winners — 16% cash was too much idle ballast while the cross-section is this cleanly ranked, so cash goes to 8% and gross from 84% to 92%. I deliberately did NOT chase bitcoin despite its +32% over the book's life: BTC is $86.7k against a $126.1k all-time high set 2025-10-06, so on the 12-month cross-sectional lookback this book ranks on it is a loser in a rebound, not a leader, and buying it would be chasing a number rather than following my own ranking. I also left the memory leg out: Micron's print was a monster (revenue $54.2bn, +350% y/y, Q1 guide $38.15 EPS) and the stock closed FLAT on it, which is distribution, not momentum — SMH gives me the complex without the single-name binary.
decisions.strategy: Cross-sectional price momentum: long the three confirmed 2026 leadership complexes — AI-capex semiconductors, AI power infrastructure, and oil-shock energy E&P — against the two cleanest measured cross-sectional losers, long-duration Treasuries and rate-killed homebuilders, with the crowded duration short trimmed after a 24-year yield high.

positions.thesis: Core expression of the strongest measured complex in the cross-section, held at top weight for the third straight leg and +3.55% on the current one. This week's tape confirmed the driver rather than the price: AI capex is being underwritten at ~$1.2T for next year, DRAM and NAND are tight enough to be setting pricing, and the Nasdaq's 10-02 gain was carried specifically by AI semiconductor leadership. 30% in a diversified 25-holding ETF is where I want concentration risk — it owns the memory and HBM upside that made Micron a $1,065 stock without exposing the book to any one blind print. Stop at 15% is wide enough to survive the late-October hyperscaler earnings (Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft) that will reprice the whole complex in either direction.

Sized up from 7% to 10% because it is the best-performing leg in the book (+5.60% in three sessions) and because the specific thing that is broadening is semiconductor materials and equipment, which is exactly what AMAT sells. Memory capex is the cleanest read-through available: Micron guided to ~$61.5bn of next-quarter revenue off tight DRAM/NAND, and that volume of memory cannot be built without wafer-fab equipment orders landing on AMAT. Adding to a winner whose fundamental driver strengthened in the same week is the core of the momentum mandate; 10% keeps it a satellite to SMH rather than a rival to it.

Held flat at 8% as the custom-ASIC and networking leg of the AI complex, +1.12% on the leg. It is the one name that monetizes hyperscaler capex through bespoke accelerators and the switching silicon between them, so it benefits from the same $1.2T capex pool as SMH but with a different revenue mechanism — that is diversification inside the complex, not duplication. Not sized up: it is the laggard of my three semi legs this leg, and the momentum rule is to add to confirmed strength, so the incremental dollar went to AMAT and GEV instead.

New leg, and the only new symbol in the book: the AI bottleneck has visibly migrated from chips to electricity, and GE Vernova is the measured price leader of that migration (+51.7% year-to-date, ~$987 on 10-01). The momentum here is backed by a hard physical constraint rather than sentiment — gas power backlog and slot reservations at 116 GW versus 83 GW at the end of 2025, and order a heavy-duty turbine today and it is delivered in 2031. That lead time is a pricing moat, and the company raised 2026 revenue guidance to $44.5-45.5bn on data-center demand. It is also a genuinely separate complex from my semis: if AI capex holds but chip margins compress, the power equipment supplier with a sold-out book still earns. Only 7% and a wider 18% stop because a stock up 52% YTD into a late-October print carries real single-name volatility, and I want the leg to survive normal noise without being stopped at the first drawdown.

Nudged 14% to 15% on the strongest macro confirmation of the week. Brent is ~$103.9 and WTI ~$91.2, crude is ~50% higher than a year ago, and the supply picture is described as the deepest global deficit in five years with conflict deployments now extended into 2027. E&P is the highest-beta cash-flow claim on that deficit, which is why I hold XOP rather than the integrated majors. The second-order point matters more for this book: energy-driven inflation is the explicit reason Treasury yields hit 24-year highs this week, so this leg and my TLT short are driven by the same engine and confirm each other. Stop at 14% respects that a headline ceasefire would hit this leg hardest and fastest.

Direction kept, size cut from 15% to 10%. The regime thesis is intact and strengthening: the 10y hit 5.33% and the 30y 5.67%, both 24-year highs, driven by energy-led inflation, a ~$40.1tn debt load, and AI data-center demand that Fed officials themselves now cite as price pressure, with the market still pricing roughly a 39% chance of an October HIKE. Being short the longest duration in a hiking regime with that supply backdrop is the right side. But I am trimming because the signal is no longer fresh: yields fell back on 10-02 after cooler PCE knocked hike odds from ~51% to ~39%, and shorting a 24-year extreme means the pain trade is a rally in bonds. At 10% weight with an 8% stop this leg risks ~0.8% of NAV, which is the right amount to pay for a crowded short I still believe in.

Sized up from 10% to 12% — this is now the cleanest measured cross-sectional loser in my opportunity set, and the only short I want to own more of. The 30-year fixed mortgage averaged 7.03% in late September and is above 7% into October, which is the direct mechanical consequence of the same 5.33% 10y that drives my TLT leg, so I am short the housing complex for the exact reason I am short duration. The confirming detail is margin destruction, not just slow volume: KB Home and Lennar say conditions have deteriorated, Lennar's average sales incentive ran ~12% of price in Q3, D.R. Horton is buying mortgage rates down to 3.99% in some markets and expects incentives to rise further in Q4. Builders funding demand out of gross margin is how a sector with falling earnings keeps printing units, and homebuilders are already down for the year. Stop at 12% caps the squeeze if a dovish surprise sparks a rate-cut rally in the most rate-sensitive sector in the market.

decisions.reason: This book's standing thesis — an inflationary hiking regime — got the strongest confirmation it has had all quarter, so the changes are about following my own logic more honestly, not about changing direction. The 10y hit 5.33% and the 30y 5.67%, both 24-year highs, the 2y is at 4.92%, and the market prices roughly a 39% chance of an October HIKE, with the stated cause being energy-driven inflation plus a ~$40.1tn debt load. That is this book's scenario happening in print. Two legs were therefore cut for contradicting it. GLD goes to zero: my own strategy of record says real yields set the gold price, and gold has now fallen from a $5,608 January high to ~$4,140 while the 10y went 5.02% to 5.34% in two weeks. J.P. Morgan's own sensitivity is roughly $20/oz per basis point of real yield, so holding 6% in the single asset most mechanically short real yields, inside a book built on real yields rising, was an unhedged contradiction. The geopolitical tail hedge it was supposed to provide is being done better and with positive carry by the energy sleeve, because the conflict risk IS the oil price here. AMGN also goes to zero: it was held as low-beta defensive ballast and it has stopped behaving that way. Its loss is idiosyncratic pipeline impairment, not market beta — Novartis's pelacarsen missed on cardiovascular outcomes, the market marked Amgen's olpasiran down on the same Lp(a) premise, the stock fell 10.08% in a day, its worst since October 2000, and it is still sliding, roughly 15% below its 03-Sep high. A binary readout on a shared scientific hypothesis is the opposite of the diversifier I wanted. The proceeds went to the leg the regime pays directly: USFR from 5% to 13%. Floating-rate Treasuries reset their coupon UP if the Fed hikes, which makes them the cleanest long expression of the live October risk and the only leg in the book that gets better if I am right about rates. VTIP 18 to 20% and XLE 12 to 14% are small adds to the two working anchors. Total one-way turnover is about 12% of the book, so I am paying a few basis points to remove two contradictions and add to the regime trade. Overlap with my Round 2 book is zero by symbol and zero by same-direction gross weight: Round 2 is long AI semis, power equipment and E&P against short duration and short homebuilders, which is a different and in places deliberately opposite expression of the same rate view.
decisions.strategy: Net-low-beta real-asset and short-duration carry for a confirmed inflationary hiking regime: a short-dated TIPS and floating-rate Treasury anchor sized up to a third of the book because a hike is now live, energy and broad-commodity cash-flow carry into the deepest oil deficit in five years, and value/min-vol/defensive-pharma risk premia — with the gold sleeve retired because real yields at 24-year highs, not inflation alone, set the gold price.

positions.thesis: Sized up from 18% to 20% as the book's largest holding and its ballast. Short-dated TIPS are the one instrument that pays me for being right about inflation without making me wrong about rates: the duration is short enough that a 5.33% 10y does little damage, while the principal accrues with a CPI that is being pushed by ~$104 Brent. That asymmetry is the whole reason this book has a -4.12% max drawdown against a book-life loss of only 0.54% while the long end made 24-year yield highs. No stop and no take-profit by design — a stop on a short-duration inflation-linked anchor would convert a volatility dampener into a thing that can be shaken out of the portfolio at the worst moment.

The main change in the book: up from 5% to 13%, funded by the GLD and AMGN exits. Floating-rate Treasury notes reset to the bill rate, so with the 2y at 4.92% and roughly a 39% market-implied chance of an October hike, this is the only leg whose income RISES in the scenario my book is positioned for, with effectively no duration to lose while it happens. It is a strictly better version of sitting in cash at 4% APY while still being short-duration — and in a regime where the market is debating a HIKE rather than a cut, paying nothing for duration is the point. No stop: a floating-rate Treasury fund has no drawdown mechanism worth stopping out of, and putting one on would be theatre.

Up from 12% to 14% and the best performer in the book (+2.15%). Brent ~$103.9 and WTI ~$91.2, crude ~50% above a year ago, and supply described as the deepest global deficit in five years with deployments extended into 2027. I hold the integrated majors here rather than high-beta E&P deliberately: this is a low-beta carry book, and XLE's dividends and buybacks turn the oil deficit into realized cash flow rather than a drilling-levered price bet. It also now doubles as the book's geopolitical tail hedge in place of gold, with the advantage of positive carry instead of a zero-coupon asset fighting 24-year-high real yields. Stop at 13% because a ceasefire headline is the one event that takes both the oil price and this leg down together.

Held at 11% as the broad-commodity complement to the single-sector energy leg, +0.43%. Its dynamic roll is the specific feature I want: in a supply-deficit market the curve backwardates, and a roll-optimized structure harvests that rather than bleeding on it, which is how a commodity index leg earns carry instead of just tracking spot. It also diversifies the inflation exposure beyond crude into metals and agriculture, which matters because the yield move this week was attributed to broad energy-driven inflation rather than one barrel price. No take-profit: this is a regime holding meant to compound through the cycle, and capping it would defeat the point of owning the inflation itself.

Held at 10%, +0.79%. This is the book's claim on the equity risk premium with the beta deliberately engineered out, which is the only form of equity exposure that belongs in a net-low-beta mandate when the S&P sits at 7,666 against a 5.33% risk-free 10y. That gap is the real risk I am managing: if the multiple compresses because the discount rate repriced rather than because earnings broke, minimum-volatility construction is what limits the damage. No stop — low-vol equity is held precisely for the drawdowns when I would otherwise be forced to sell, and a stop would force exactly that sale.

Held at 9%, +1.11%. Value is the factor with the shortest implied duration in equities — the cash flows arrive sooner, so a 5.33% discount rate hurts it least, and it is structurally the right factor premium to own when the long bond is making 24-year yield highs. It is also the cleanest counterweight inside my own mandate to the long-duration growth complex that my Round 2 book is long, which keeps the two books genuinely independent expressions rather than one bet in two wrappers. No stop: factor premia are harvested across cycles and get stopped out at precisely the wrong point in them.

Held at 7% and now the larger of the two remaining pharma legs after the AMGN exit, down only 0.70%. It stays because its small loss is ordinary sector beta rather than an impaired thesis — unlike Amgen, it has no exposure to the failed Lp(a) hypothesis that broke that leg. Large-cap pharma earns its place here on cash-flow durability and inelastic demand, which is the kind of defensive income this book wants when the discount rate is 5.33%. Stop at 13% because US drug-pricing policy remains a live top-line risk for the sector that no amount of balance-sheet quality hedges.

Held at 6% despite being 2.89% underwater, deliberately not sized up and deliberately not cut. The drawdown is sector drift from a week when pharma was marked down on an Lp(a) read-across that has nothing to do with Gilead's HIV and virology franchise, so cutting it would be selling an unrelated asset for someone else's trial failure — the same error in reverse that kept AMGN too long. Its franchise cash flows are about as rate-insensitive and recession-insensitive as listed equity gets, which is the defensive premium this sleeve exists to hold. Kept at 6% rather than larger because after retiring AMGN I want the pharma sleeve at 13% of the book in total, not rebuilt to its old size. Stop at 13% for the same drug-pricing policy risk that caps the MRK leg.

decisions.reason: One dated fact changed this book and one confirmed it. The change: on 2026-10-02 Toshiba announced roughly Y60bn of capex to double HDD output by fiscal 2027 and to lift share from just over 10% toward 30% medium-term, and WDC fell hard on it. HDD pricing power was never a demand story - it was a three-player supply-discipline story - so a declared share grab attacks the premise of the WDC leg rather than just the multiple. WDC was already the only broken chart in my complex, roughly halved from its June high near $800 to $415 while MU printed records and SNDK ran about 700% in 2026, and it was my worst leg at -7.3%. I am cutting it to zero rather than averaging into relative weakness, because the supply response the whole mandate fears has now actually shown up - in HDDs specifically, and nowhere else I own. The confirmation: the bits thesis got better. Micron now shows 6.09x forward earnings on $133bn of revenue up 256% year over year, $85bn of net income, record DRAM revenue with pricing up high-teens, 26 supply-and-capacity agreements carrying $12.7bn of customer deposits and more than 75% of 2027 output already committed. On the supply side new fabs cannot reach meaningful volume before 2027-2028, NAND capacity is being structurally cut to roughly 40% below the 2022 peak by 2027, and BofA has pushed its cycle-peak estimate to end-2027. So I am concentrating, not diversifying. I considered adding AMAT as a second equipment leg and rejected it: at roughly 39x forward it fails my own mandate, which is to own the CHEAPEST bottleneck, and its own house target of $550 sits barely above the $540 price. Three legs in one bottleneck, cash drag cut from 14% to 10%, and wide stops because this is where the volatility is.
decisions.strategy: A three-leg, 90%-invested bet on the cheapest bottleneck in the AI buildout - DRAM and NAND bits at single-digit forward earnings - with the hard-drive leg cut outright after Toshiba moved to double HDD supply, and the proceeds concentrated into Micron at 6x forward plus one wafer-fab-equipment leg as the second-derivative claim on the memory capex those bit margins are now funding.

positions.thesis: The mandate in one name: the cheapest bottleneck AND the one with contracted visibility. 6.09x forward earnings on $133bn revenue up 256% and $85bn net income, record $39.8bn DRAM quarter with prices up high-teens, 26 supply-and-capacity agreements holding $12.7bn of customer deposits, over 75% of 2027 output pre-sold, against a 49-analyst Strong Buy and a $1,520 average target. Sized largest - up from 34% - because it is simultaneously the cheapest leg, the most diversified across DRAM, HBM and NAND, and the most pre-sold, so it carries the least spot-pricing risk per dollar of earnings. It is also the one leg with earnings behind it rather than ahead of it this month. Take-profit at 50% sits just above the street's average target.

The purest listed claim on NAND, and NAND is the half of memory where supply is being cut rather than added: suppliers are prioritizing DRAM, and 2027 NAND capacity is projected about 40% below the 2022 peak. Consensus looks for roughly $43 of quarterly EPS on $10.5bn revenue on 10/29, versus $1.22 and $2.31bn a year earlier, which is near 10x forward even after a ~700% year. Held and nudged up from 26% in weight terms only because WDC's cash had to go somewhere - but deliberately not made the biggest leg, because a parabolic chart into an earnings print is the wrong place for maximum size. Stop set wide at 28% because this name's daily range is large enough that a conventional stop would be noise, not risk control.

The second-derivative leg, sized up from 12% because its own guidance moved and because the capex is now provably coming: Lam raised CY2026 wafer-fab equipment to $140bn, and the industry is directing more spend to DRAM than NAND, which is precisely where Lam's etch and deposition franchise is most levered. If record bit margins fund new fabs - and the shortage leaves suppliers no choice - this is where that money lands. Already my best leg at +15.1%, with a 10/21 print as the next catalyst. Held to 21% rather than larger because at roughly 43x NTM EV/EBITDA it is the expensive leg in a book whose edge is cheapness.

decisions.reason: Nothing in this book is broken, and the one thing I could change I do not want to. The leg is three trading days old (entered 2026-09-30), the book is +11.89% lifetime, and all six legs are at or above entry. Every premise got confirmed rather than challenged. Copper, my largest leg at 22%, is the cleanest: LME three-month set a record $14,858.50/tonne and has printed successive intraday records since, COMEX made a record $6.894/lb, copper is up roughly 48% over one year, and COPX has absorbed about $1.7bn of 2026 inflows on exactly the AI-electricity argument I rebuilt this book around. GEV +4.0%, PWR +5.3% and ETN +1.5% are all working on record grid backlogs with nothing in the tape against them. I specifically re-examined the two legs I had doubts about and am keeping both. GDX is flat and gold has had two down weeks near $4,140, pressured by the oil-driven inflation path rather than by anything wrong with miners - but miners sit at 15.3x earnings with central-bank buying intact and spot recovering from a first-half correction, which is a laggard to be patient with, not a thesis to abandon in the week a shooting war could gap it. XLE is the harder call: Hormuz has been closed since May, Washington has now rejected Iran's reopen-for-blockade-lift proposal, Brent is near $100-103, a third carrier group plus 10,000 troops land by end-November, and Trump is telegraphing resumed strikes after the November midterms. That is a real catalyst - but it is roughly seven weeks out, the escalation premium is already in a $100 print, and I get to revisit this book every week between now and then. Being early into an oil shock at record copper is not a free option. The deliberate choice is to leave the 18% cash alone. It is the reason this book's max drawdown is -6.09% against my Round 2 book's -15.25%, I would be deploying it into copper at all-time highs after a 48% year with sell-side already warning the rally could cool, and a full replacement costs real basis points at 2bps a side plus SEC/TAF to re-buy the same six names in nearly the same sizes. Churning a three-day-old book into the strength of its own thesis is paying frictions to reset my stops higher up.

Nothing this week falsified a premise in this book; every one of the four legs got externally confirmed, and all four are only two trading days old (filled 09-30). XLV at 38% is the core and the tape backs it: the sector is up ~9% over the past month and ~16% over three months, outpacing the S&P, on rotation out of crowded AI/tech into defensive growth, accelerating sector earnings, a biotech resurgence, and roughly $284bn of 2026 sector M&A as large pharma buys pipeline ahead of the 2028 patent cliff. The drug-pricing overhang that this book was repositioned around has not come back; commentators now describe the de-risking as a precedent for how a regulated industry and the government coexist. The leg's -1.33% mark is two days of giveback after a 9% month, not a thesis break, and I will not pay frictions to sell a sector whose fundamentals improved. XLE (+2.15%) is likewise confirmed harder than when I set it: Brent ~$99.7 and WTI ~$91 with Brent up ~54% year-on-year, OPEC+ expected to leave production targets unchanged, and analysts raising 2026 forecasts because a quick normalization of Strait of Hormuz shipping no longer looks likely. That is the physical-crude tightness the leg was sized for. QUAL and USMV are the right factor tilts for exactly this week's tape: the 10-year hit 5.34% intraday (highest since 2002), the 30-year reached 24-year highs, and the 5-year cleared 5% for the first time since 2007 on fiscal and term-premium concerns, while the Nasdaq simultaneously printed a record 30,808. Strong balance sheets and low realized beta are what you want when the long end is repricing under a record-high index. The 22% cash also still earns what I underwrote it for: fed funds is 3.75-4.00% after the September hike, and futures price ~4.1% by January and ~4.7% by October 2027, so the risk-free rate is paid and still rising even though the weak September jobs report (29k, unemployment 4.2%) cut October hike odds from ~64% to ~21%. An October pause is one meeting, not the end of the cycle, so I am not reaching for duration or for yield-proxy risk. I am aware this book is +0.73% against SPY +2.78%, but trailing a melt-up is the designed cost of a low-beta defensive mandate, not evidence the book is wrong; with VIX at 15.3 and realized 30-day vol at 10.5 under a record index and a 24-year-high long bond, holding dry powder is a position. Churning four two-day-old confirmed legs to close a relative-performance gap would be paying real basis points to chase beta I am explicitly not mandated to own.

One premise in this book broke this week and one got much stronger, so I am making a single surgical swap rather than another full rebuild - this book is on leg 11 in 12 weeks and over-trading is part of why it sits at -0.80%. What broke is BKLN. I bought floating-rate loan carry last week for coupons that reset upward with the policy rate, and all three legs of that case weakened at once. First, the reset kicker is now hostage to a Fed that is pausing: the weak September jobs report (29k jobs, unemployment up to 4.2%) cut October hike odds from ~64% to ~21%, with Williams saying there is 'no need for urgency' and Jefferson wanting 'more time'. Second, the credit side is deteriorating into the exact window I am holding - Fitch's trailing-12-month leveraged loan default rate was 3.8% in July and Fitch expects 4.5-5.0% by year-end against a 3.4% historical average, and the premium to lend to B- borrowers is the widest since the onset of COVID. Third, there is little historical precedent for loan spreads to tighten further, so the only route to higher loan prices is a LOWER SOFR base rate, which is the one thing that also kills the coupon. A carry leg whose spread cannot tighten, whose coupon only rises if the Fed keeps hiking, and whose defaults are forecast to rise either way is not carry I am being paid for. I am taking the 13% out. What got stronger is the commodity-inflation engine, but I deliberately did NOT recycle BKLN's weight into it. Brent is ~$99.7 and WTI ~$91, Brent is up ~54% year-on-year, OPEC+ is expected to hold production targets, and forecasters are raising 2026 numbers because quick normalization of Strait of Hormuz shipping no longer looks likely. That is why PDBC, AMLP and XOP all stay. But PDBC's index is itself energy-heavy, so PDBC+AMLP+XOP already means a single Hormuz de-escalation headline marks down 43% of this book at once, and that correlation is the real risk here, not the direction. So the replacement is GLD at 14%, which keeps the inflation and fiscal-debasement exposure while unloading the Hormuz risk premium. The regime argues for it directly: the 10-year hit 5.34% intraday (highest since 2002), the 30-year is at 24-year highs and the 5-year cleared 5% for the first time since 2007, driven by fiscal concern and term premium rather than by growth - that is the setup gold is paid in. Gold also rallied back through $4,190 on the same jobs print that hurt my loan leg, so it hedges the pause my other legs dislike. I am keeping the hiking-cycle tilt generally, because futures still price fed funds at ~4.1% by January and ~4.7% by October 2027 off 3.75-4.00% today; an October pause is one meeting, not a pivot. Cash stays at 10% at 4%.
decisions.strategy: Cross-asset carry and trend stacking with the floating-rate loan carry leg closed on deteriorating loan credit and replaced by a gold trend sleeve, keeping weight in the engines a still-tightening Fed and supply-driven commodity inflation actually pay - commodity backwardation carry, systematic managed-futures trend, midstream and E&P energy carry, and an equity variance-premium sleeve - all long-only.

positions.thesis: The core commodity-carry engine and the leg with the strongest physical confirmation in the book. Broad commodity carry only pays when the curve is backwardated, and the oil curve is backwardated for a supply reason that is persisting rather than resolving: Brent ~$99.7 and WTI ~$91, Brent up ~54% year-on-year, OPEC+ expected to leave production targets unchanged at its meeting of eight members, and a Reuters poll of analysts marking 2026 Brent up to ~$89 average because hopes for a quick normalization of Strait of Hormuz shipping have faded. PDBC's no-K-1 optimum-yield structure rolls into the backwardated part of the curve, so I collect roll yield as well as spot. I trimmed 1pt from 23% to 22% only to fund the gold sleeve, not because conviction fell. Sized below last week's level in spirit because PDBC's index is energy-heavy and this book already owns AMLP and XOP against the same Hormuz headline; 22% is as much of that single correlated risk as I want in the largest leg. Stop 12% because a Hormuz de-escalation is a real and fast tail, take-profit 25% to bank a genuine supply spike rather than round-trip it.

The systematic trend sleeve and the one leg that does not need me to be right about direction. DBMF replicates managed-futures positioning, and the two trends that dominate right now are exactly the ones the tape is delivering: long commodities into a supply-driven crude move, and short duration into a long end repricing to multi-decade highs (10-year 5.27% after a 5.34% intraday print, 30-year at 24-year highs, 5-year above 5% for the first time since 2007). It also holds the one structural advantage in this book - it is the only position that can flip its own sign. If the Hormuz premium unwinds and crude breaks, the trend model reverses and goes short the commodity complex while PDBC, AMLP and XOP are all losing, which is why I keep it at the same 22% as PDBC rather than behind it. Kept at full weight and unchanged; +1.17% on the current leg. Stop 12% and no take-profit on purpose - a trend sleeve is only worth owning if I let the convex right tail run, and a take-profit would cut exactly the payoff I am buying.

New leg, funded by closing BKLN plus 1pt from PDBC. This is the trend half of the mandate taking over weight from carry I am no longer paid for, and its job is to hold the inflation and debasement exposure without adding to the Hormuz concentration. The driver stack is live and distinct from crude: the long end is at multi-decade highs (30-year at 24-year highs, 5-year over 5% for the first time since 2007) on fiscal and term-premium concern rather than on growth, which is historically the cleanest environment for gold, and gold is in a powerful multi-year uptrend trading around $4,140-4,218 on 10-02. Critically it hedges the one macro event that hurts the rest of this book: gold rebounded through $4,190 on the very September jobs print that cut October hike odds to ~21% and undercut my floating-rate coupon thesis, so a dovish surprise that compresses my carry legs is a tailwind here. Sized at 14% rather than larger because gold's own carry is negative (no coupon, no roll yield) and DBMF is likely already long it, so this is deliberately a diversifier and not a second core. Stop 12%, roughly gold's annualized vol, and no take-profit so the trend can run.

Midstream distribution carry - the highest-quality cash coupon left in the book now that the loan leg is gone, and the one energy leg that is paid on volumes and fee-based contracts rather than on the flat price of crude. With Brent near $100, OPEC+ holding targets and US producers having every incentive to move barrels, throughput and the distributions it funds are well supported, and MLP distribution yields clear my 4% cash rate by a wide margin, which is the actual test for a carry sleeve. Unchanged at 12% and +1.48% on the current leg. I kept it rather than rotating it because its payoff is structurally less flat-price-sensitive than XOP's, so it is the more defensible of my two equity energy legs if the Hormuz premium deflates. Stop 12%, no take-profit: this leg is held to collect the coupon, so capping the price upside would cut the return without reducing the risk I actually carry.

The equity variance-premium sleeve, kept at 11% because I checked whether the premium is actually being paid rather than assuming it. It is: VIX closed at 15.31 on 10-02 against realized 30-day volatility of 10.51, a spread of roughly five vol points, which is a healthy variance risk premium and precisely the gap a covered-call overlay monetizes. Writing calls at implied 15 against a tape realizing 10.5 is positive-expectancy carry, and JEPI's underlying is a low-volatility quality equity screen rather than the crowded AI complex that led the market to its record 30,808 Nasdaq close. I am clear on the cost: JEPI caps upside, so in a continued melt-up this is the leg that lags, and that is why it stays at 11% and is not sized up. Stop 10%, tighter than the rest of the book, because a covered-call fund gives up upside and so has no mechanism to recover a deep drawdown quickly; if equity vol regime-shifts upward the premium collected will not cover the delta and I want out early.

The highest-beta expression of the crude thesis and the best-performing leg in the book at +3.12% in two sessions. XOP is equal-weighted E&P, so it is levered to the flat price in a way AMLP is not: with Brent ~$99.7 and WTI ~$91 and analysts raising 2026 forecasts on a Hormuz disruption that is dragging on while OPEC+ withholds supply, producer free cash flow at these strip prices is very large relative to where the names are valued. Deliberately the smallest equity leg at 9% and left unchanged - this is the right vehicle for the thesis but the wrong one to concentrate in, because it is the third position in this book exposed to the same single headline, and equal-weight E&P drops hardest if that headline turns. Wide 15% stop because E&P noise would trigger anything tighter and I would be stopped out of a thesis that was still intact, with a 30% take-profit to force me to actually bank a geopolitical spike instead of holding it into the de-escalation.

decisions.reason: Three things changed. (1) The inflation shock my mandate told me to hedge has actually arrived and it is an energy shock: WTI $91 and Brent $100, both roughly +50% year-over-year, with core PCE marked up to 3.4% and the Fed hiking to 3.75-4.00% in September for the first time since 2023. (2) It now comes with a growth crack: September payrolls were 29K against 84K expected, July revised to -10K, unemployment 4.2%. That combination is stagflation, and in stagflation a 20% cash buffer earning 4% against 3%+ inflation is not safety, it is a slow loss. I cut cash to 15% and moved the proceeds into real assets. (3) Two legs were contradicting my own strategy of record. PEP was a bond-proxy staple I had already said I was moving away from, and it is now down ~10% YTD, ~24% from its high, with JPMorgan cutting to Neutral and Frito-Lay's recovery stalled -- cheap, but broken, and a value trap rather than a mean-reversion candidate. QCOM's cheapness no longer holds either: consensus is Hold, the mean target of ~$191 is essentially where it trades, and the Apple content loss is structural, not cyclical. Both are gone. In their place I added physical gold, which is the asset actually responding to this regime (bullion ~$4,170 after a $4,690 futures peak, an ~11% pullback inside an intact uptrend -- a contrarian entry into a confirmed hedge), and I concentrated harder into the one cluster where cheapness, quality, a live catalyst and defensiveness all coincide: managed care at 30% of the book. I deliberately did NOT buy gold miners here for this book; GDX is at decade highs and is a momentum instrument, not a value one, so the value book takes the metal and leaves the equity beta alone.
decisions.strategy: Contrarian value in capitulated quality, concentrated in the managed-care margin-recovery trade and cheap cash-flow IT, with the mandated inflation-shock hedge upgraded from staples-and-crypto to integrated energy plus physical gold now that an oil-driven stagflation is the confirmed regime.

positions.thesis: My largest position and the core of the book. The margin-recovery thesis is no longer a hope: FY26 adjusted EPS guidance was raised to $19.50-$20.00 and management is deliberately shedding 1.3-1.4m Medicare Advantage lives to buy back margin rather than defend volume, which is exactly the capital discipline a contrarian wants to see from a capitulated compounder. The stock is up ~40% from its March lows and still sits at $371.90 against a $480 mean target with 19 of 26 analysts at Strong Buy, so the re-rating is only partly done. It is also the right thing to own into a weakening labour market: healthcare utilisation is non-discretionary and the revenue is not consumer-cyclical. Upsized from 14% because this is my highest-conviction idea and the brief imposes no position cap.

The cheapest high-quality name I could find anywhere in this market: a 9.6x forward P/E, roughly half the sector average, on $30.50 of 2026 consensus EPS. It rides the same moderating-medical-cost-trend tailwind that is re-rating the whole MCO group (covered managed-care shares up ~35% on average since September 2025) but has participated far less, which is the definition of the mean-reversion setup this book exists to own. Pairing it with UNH makes managed care 30% of the book -- intentional concentration into one thesis expressed through the premium operator and the deep-value operator, so I am paid whether the group re-rates on earnings delivery or on multiple catch-up.

The primary expression of the mandated inflation-shock hedge, and it is now hedging a shock that is actually happening rather than a hypothetical one. Brent at ~$100 and WTI at ~$91, both up about 50% year-over-year, is the proximate cause of the 3.4% core PCE that forced the Fed's hand, so this leg is long the thing that is driving the macro pain in every other asset I own. Integrated energy is still priced well below what $90+ crude implies for mid-cycle free cash flow, which keeps it inside a value mandate rather than being a momentum chase. Added a point and left the take-profit off deliberately: a hedge against an open-ended inflation shock should not be capped, and capping it last quarter is the kind of thing that makes a hedge stop working exactly when you need it.

Working as intended at +6.87% and retained near full size. Cheap IT services is the right kind of cash-flow value for a stagflation: the revenue is contracted and recurring, the business is asset-light so there is little input-cost exposure to $91 oil, and corporate AI implementation spend is a genuine demand tailwind rather than a cost line. Trimmed a point only to fund the gold hedge, not because the thesis weakened.

New leg, and the single most important change in this book. My mandate requires an inflation-shock hedge, and gold is the asset that is actually responding to this one: bullion ran from below $4,000 in late June to above $4,600 in August and sits ~$4,170 now, an ~11% pullback inside an unbroken uptrend, which is a contrarian entry rather than a breakout chase. It hedges the specific thing cash cannot: a Fed that is hiking into 3.4% core inflation and has just been handed a 29K payroll print, which is the setup where real yields fall, policy credibility is questioned, and the metal re-rates. I chose the bullion trust over the miners on purpose -- GDX is at decade highs and up 53% year-over-year, so miners are a momentum instrument whose cheapness has already been arbitraged away, while GLD gives me the hedge with no operating leverage, no single-asset risk and no equity beta bleeding into a book that is already 30% long one equity theme.

The second leg of the energy hedge, held alongside XOM to spread single-name operational risk across two integrateds rather than concentrating the mandate's hedge in one balance sheet. Up 1.48% since entry, with a dividend and buyback profile that is comfortably covered at $90 crude. Added a point as part of shifting cash into real assets; no take-profit, for the same reason as XOM.

The purest capitulated-quality setup left in the book, so I added to it on weakness instead of cutting the loser. Q3 was a beat on both lines -- $6.13 EPS against $6.08, revenue $6.76bn up 12.9% -- and management raised full-year guidance to $26.58-26.63bn revenue and $24.45-24.50 EPS, yet the stock is down 4.74% on my leg. The market is paying for the generative-AI competitive narrative and refusing to pay for accelerating reported results, which is exactly the gap mean-reversion harvests. I keep it small and give it a wide 18% stop because the bear case, that AI genuinely compresses creative-software pricing, is a real structural risk and not one I can disprove.

Trimmed from 4% to 3% and kept only as a token hard-asset leg. The honest assessment is that it has not done its job: BTC is up 32% over this book's life while ETH has gone sideways and is down 3.90% on my leg, so as a debasement hedge it has been dominated by both bitcoin and gold. It has at least just broken out of the $2,600 range it held since September 24 to ~$2,757 on short liquidations and easing front-end yields, so I am not selling into the one piece of good news it has had. But the capital it was really holding belongs in GLD, which is why the gold leg is 11% and this one is 3%. The 35bps round-trip on crypto is also a reason to shrink rather than churn it.

decisions.reason: This book is down 3.83% while SPY is up 3.80%, and the research says plainly why: it called itself 'a trend book that finally owns the trends that exist' and was then positioned SHORT the single strongest trend in the market. GDX is up 53% over the past year, up 18% in a month, at decade highs, and has compounded about 49% a year over three years against 30% for bullion, with gold itself having run from under $4,000 in June to above $4,600 in August. My own leg thesis described a 'real-yield-driven gold-miner downtrend'. There is no such downtrend. That premise was simply false, and the honest fix is not to trim the short but to reverse it -- so GDX goes from 7% short to 15% long, and it is now the clearest trend-following expression in the book. The second change is consolidating duration. I was short 29% gross across TLT and EDV, which is one bet wearing two tickers, and EDV's ~24-year duration is the leg with the most convexity against me. The long-end trend is intact and I am staying with it -- 30Y at 5.636% is a 24-year high and 10Y at 5.344% the highest since April 2002 -- and the curve behaved like a stagflation curve on 10-02, with the 2Y rallying 10bps on the weak jobs print while 30Y only gave back 4bps after setting that high, which is exactly the shape that rewards being short the long end rather than the front. But a 29K payroll print against 84K expected, negative July revisions and 4.2% unemployment are a real growth-scare risk to any duration short, so I cut the duration short from 29% to 17% and hold it only in TLT. Third, I replaced the reversed gold short with a short that is actually in a downtrend: XLY, where consumer discretionary is the worst S&P sector of 2026 at -8.7% with softening revenue and free cash flow and weak consumer confidence, now joined by a cracking labour market and $91 crude taxing the same wallet. That keeps my short book from being a pure undiversified rates bet. Energy goes from 8% to 14% because it is simultaneously the strongest sector trend and the only leg that pays me in the one scenario -- an uncontained oil-driven inflation shock -- that would hurt the factor longs and the duration short at the same time.
decisions.strategy: A trend book that stops fighting the strongest trend on the tape: long the momentum and quality factors, long energy and now long gold miners, short the long end of the Treasury curve where yields sit at 24-year highs, and short the consumer discretionary sector that a 29K payroll print just confirmed as the weakest fundamental trend in the market.

positions.thesis: Still the anchor long and still working at +1.75% since entry. The US momentum factor is the cleanest systematic way to own whatever is trending without having to forecast which theme wins, and in this tape its constituents capture the AI complex, energy and precious metals strength at once, with the factor rebalancing into leadership rather than requiring me to. Held near full size and trimmed only two points to fund the energy increase. The 12% stop is the trend-following discipline: momentum's failure mode is a sharp factor reversal, and the only sane response to that is to be stopped out of it rather than to argue with it.

The rates trend is intact and this is where I keep it, consolidated out of the old TLT-plus-EDV pair into the single most liquid long-end instrument. 30-year yields printed 5.636%, a 24-year high, and 10-year yields 5.344%, the highest since April 2002, while the Fed has hiked to 3.75-4.00% with core PCE marked to 3.4% and the median dot still implying another hike. Critically, the 10-02 session showed the stagflation curve shape rather than a bull-flattening: the 2Y rallied 10bps on the soft payroll print while the 30Y surrendered only 4bps of a fresh 24-year-high yield, so weak growth is being expressed at the front end and inflation-plus-fiscal risk premium is keeping the long end offered. That is the configuration that pays a long-end short. Cut from 29% gross to 17% and kept the tight 8% stop because the clear risk -- a 29K payroll print turning into a genuine growth scare that rallies the entire curve -- is live, and this is the leg that loses most if it does.

A full reversal of last week's short, and the correction this book most needed. The short was built on a 'real-yield-driven gold-miner downtrend' that does not exist: GDX is up 53% year-over-year, up 18% over the past month, sitting at decade highs near $88, having compounded roughly 49% annually over three years against bullion's 30% -- the operating leverage is running the right way, with Newmont +20.6% and Agnico +22.9% in a single breakout week. A trend book has no business being short that. It is also the position that fits the macro: a central bank hiking into 3.4% core inflation and then receiving a 29K payroll print is the textbook setup for falling real yields and a monetary-debasement bid for gold. I am entering on a pullback -- bullion ~$4,170 against an August futures peak near $4,690, GDX off its $89.73 spike -- rather than at the high. Sized 15% rather than larger, and given a wide 15% stop with a 40% take-profit, because miner beta to the metal cuts both ways and this is the most volatile instrument in the book.

Nearly doubled from 8% to 14% because it is doing two jobs at once. As a trend, it is among the strongest sectors on the tape: WTI ~$91 and Brent ~$100 are up about 50% year-over-year, Brent is up 4.36% in the past month, and consensus has Brent at $113 by quarter-end on tighter supply and geopolitical risk. As insurance, it is the only leg that pays me in the single scenario that damages everything else simultaneously -- an inflation shock that re-accelerates, forcing the Fed to hike harder, which would hit MTUM and QUAL through the discount rate and could eventually break even the long-end short by crushing growth. Paying up for that correlation profile is worth more than the 2bps of frictions it costs to resize.

Retained but cut from 18% to 12%. The quality factor is doing its job at +1.01% and it is the right factor to hold into a slowing labour market, since strong balance sheets and stable margins are what survive a stagflation with financing costs at 24-year highs. The reason for the trim is honest redundancy: quality and momentum overlap heavily in their current holdings, so 46% across the two was paying twice for one exposure, and the released capital does more work in gold miners and energy, which are genuinely uncorrelated with the factor longs.

The new short, and it replaces the reversed gold short with a downtrend that is actually real. Consumer discretionary is the worst-performing S&P 500 sector of 2026 at -8.7%, and unlike most oversold readings this one has deteriorating fundamentals behind it -- softer revenue and free cash flow, weak consumer confidence -- rather than just a drawdown. The 10-02 data made the case stronger, not weaker: 29K payrolls against 84K expected, July revised to a 10K loss, unemployment up to 4.2%, temporary help down 11K, and average hourly earnings up just 0.1% to $37.81, which is wage growth running below inflation. A squeezed consumer facing $91 crude at the pump and 24-year-high financing costs is the clearest fundamental short available. Kept deliberately small at 8% with a tight 10% stop, because XLY's cap-weighted megacap constituents mean it is partly correlated with my MTUM long, so I want this as a diversifying hedge on the weakest trend, not as a second big directional bet.
